Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature
articles.description: A U.S. startup is seeking $162 million in damages and an injunction to impact iPhone and Apple Watch imports to India.
articles.content: Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology. GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch. Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims. In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The company launched StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024. Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1. “We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing. In the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale. Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android. Apple did not respond to a request for comment. India has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino company has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth. articles.title: Zohran Mamdani makes surprise appearance on CNN’s ‘Have I Got News for You’
articles.content: “We’re gonna have someone fun come out,” Roy Wood Jr. told the studio audience for CNN’s comedy panel show “Have I Got News for You” on Friday afternoon. Judging by the cheers and applause, the audience was happily surprised by what happened next. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined Wood on stage for a jovial conversation about politics, including the Senate leadership race and the mayor’s much-scrutinized relationship with President Donald Trump. The episode, which will air Saturday at 9 p.m. Eastern on CNN, demonstrated the in-demand mayor’s unconventional approach to media appearances While he hasn’t appeared on “Saturday Night Live,” he dropped by “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” when Kimmel was in Brooklyn last September, and made a cameo on “The Tonight Show” soon after his inauguration in January. “This is crazy. I was actually here to see John Oliver,” Mamdani joked during the CNN taping, knowing that Oliver’s HBO show is taped in the same building on the far west side of Manhattan. The timing of Friday’s “Have I Got News for You” visit was notable for a couple of reasons. First, it was one of Mamdani’s first interviews since the Democratic Party retook control of Congress in the midterm elections; second, it was slightly complicated by the fact that Mamdani is on crutches right now. On Thursday evening, the mayor sustained an injury during a soccer game with members of the New York City press corps. “I tore my Achilles,” he told reporters at a press conference Friday morning. “Have I Got News for You” producers worried that he might cancel, but Mamdani still participated in the taping, seated at the table with his crutches kept off-screen. “I got scared when you showed up, because usually when you show up in New York, it’s to fix something,” Wood said, making a joke about his own job security. Then Wood and his panelists pretended to continue with the show as planned, beginning with the question, “Can Mamdani pull off this mustache?” The mayor explained that he is participating in “Movember” to raise awareness about men’s health issues. Panelist Amber Ruffin sounded smitten. “You’re Homecoming king right now,” she quipped. “And maybe, always?” The comedians offered theories about Trump’s unexpectedly cordial working relationship with Mamdani. “It’s like, you know that old Life cereal commercial? ‘Mikey hates everything, but he likes Life.’ I feel like that’s Trump with you,” panelist Michael Ian Black said. Mamdani posited that “the one thing we do have in common is this city,” given Trump is a native New Yorker; whenever they talk, the mayor said, “I try and focus our conversations around housing, how to build more housing.” Mamdani let the professionals crack most of the jokes. When the show turned to Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who recently urged Trump to embrace Medicare for All as “Trumpcare,” Black remarked, “If Trump goes for El-Sayed’s pitch, and he’s a fan of yours, is there any chance we could convert him to Islam?” Mamdani laughed, smiled and waited a beat while thinking about what to say. “It’s never come up in our conversations,” he responded. Mamdani also weighed in on Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s challenge against Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Schumer declined to endorse Mamdani for mayor last year, and Mamdani hasn’t backed Schumer in the majority leader contest. Black asked him: “Do you have a preference?” “I think less about who it should be and more about what they should do,” Mamdani said, arguing that “the point of power is to use it, to deliver.” Mamdani stayed on message and avoided direct criticism of Schumer. Later in the conversation, he said, “I don’t think grudges are worth holding, because grudges don’t pay people’s bills. And to me, I think that our politics has to be, how do we help New Yorkers pay their bills?”

Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, former South Africa deputy president and UN Women chief, dies at 71
articles.content: JOHANNESBURG (AP) — Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president and a United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at age 71, the South African government announced Friday. Mlambo-Ngcuka, a former anti-apartheid activist and lawmaker in the South African Parliament, was deputy president from 2005 until 2008. She also served as minister of minerals and energy and deputy minister of trade and industry. She served as under-secretary-general and executive director of U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021. The exact date and location of her death were not immediately shared by the government or her political party, the African National Congress. Mlambo-Ngcuka was part of South Africa’s first democratic Parliament for the ANC after the end of apartheid and white minority rule in 1994 when Nelson Mandela was elected the country’s first democratically elected leader. Tributes following her death lauded her contribution to South Africa’s struggle for liberation and new democracy and the role she played at the U.N., where she championed women’s rights and gender equality. “Mama Phumzile was a distinguished leader of our movement and a dedicated servant of the people. She made history as the first woman to serve as Deputy President of South Africa,” the ANC said in a statement Friday. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres expressed condolences and called her “a lifelong champion of the rights and empowerment of women and girls.” “Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka’s fight began long before she entered the world stage. As a young teacher in KwaZulu-Natal and an activist against apartheid, she learned that freedom is never complete until it reaches every woman and every girl,” he said in a statement Friday. U.N. Women said her courage inspired people around the world and her leadership helped shape a global movement. “From her early days as an anti-apartheid activist to becoming South Africa’s first woman Deputy President, and later leading U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021, she devoted her life to justice and equality,” the agency said in a statement. Mlambo-Ngcuka was appointed deputy president during a volatile era in South African politics and for the ruling ANC, which was experiencing infighting and a bruising succession battle. She replaced former Deputy President Jacob Zuma when he was fired after being implicated in a corruption scandal involving an arms deal. Despite her known history as a political activist and experienced lawmaker, her appointment drew criticism over her marriage to Bulelani Ngcuka, the country’s lead prosecutor who was pursuing corruption charges against Zuma. She is survived by her husband and their five children.

Michigan Supreme Court upholds renewable energy law over townships' challenge
articles.description: The Michigan Supreme Court declined an appeal from dozens of townships that want to turn back state rules allowing renewable energy projects to bypass local governments and get approval from the state.
articles.content: Escanaba put over 3 thousand panels at the Delta County Airport in 2019. Only 637 have been sold since then, but the city says it has saved over $500 thousand in energy purchase costs and over $100 in transmission costs. (City of Escanaba Electric Department)Both sides of a lawsuit over Michigan’s renewable energy zoning law are claiming victory at the state Supreme Court.A state law enacted in 2023, known as P.A. 233, lets the state preempt local zoning and approve renewable energy projects, but only if local rules are too strict. The Michigan Public Service Commission found that to mean ordinances that went beyond regulations listed in the law, covering issues like fencing, height, and sound.Dozens of Michigan townships challenged the interpretation and lost that battle at the Court of Appeals. Friday, the Supreme Court released an order that upheld most of the law.The Michigan Energy Innovation Business Council was among the environmental groups seeking to protect the policy in court.President Laura Sherman said it incentivizes projects to work with local governments rather than around them, especially since going to the state could get expensive and would likely require paying several fees to the local governments anyway.She argued local governments also have a reason to cooperate.“If you want to be assured that a project cannot go to the state, then you set up a local ordinance that has these very clear requirements," Sherman said. "Today, [it] has been affirmed by the Supreme Court that those are the simple requirements,” Sherman said.In a press release, the lawyers for the townships said they were disappointed in that decision. Other parts of the ruling, however, gave them reason to celebrate.The Public Service Commission originally decided only the local governments that had zoning authority over a proposed site counted as an “affected local unit” that could negotiate with energy companies seeking to locate a renewable project there. The Court of Appeals and Michigan Supreme Court both found that definition too narrow.Instead, they considered any local unit of government that the project touched as affected.Foster Swift lawyer Michael D. Homier is lead attorney on the case for the townships.“This is an important win for counties and other local governments that may not exercise zoning authority over a project site but will nevertheless experience the project’s impacts,” Homier said in a press release. “The decision confirms that those communities cannot be excluded from the rights and protections the Legislature provided under PA 233 simply because another local government exercises zoning jurisdiction.”While settling some of those issues, the Michigan Supreme Court did set the table for oral arguments about timing. In January, the sides will come together to discuss how long local governments have to respond to developers.Sherman said regardless of what the court decides, the local governments couldn’t delay forever.“The intent of the Legislature was really clear, that you want to give local governments the opportunity to regulate these projects, but if you choose not to do that, they cannot delay in perpetuity, that was one of the reasons that this law passed in the first place,” she said.

Walled Lake considers school closure amid declining enrollment
articles.description: The potential closure of Central High School is a proposed response to declining enrollment — an issue faced by many districts in the state and the country.
articles.content: Plainwell Community Schools is one of several Michigan schools with a bond request on the November ballot. The district says funds are needed to ensure doors and windows keep out intruders, build a new preschool and more. Voters already rejected a version of their proposal in May.(Plainwell Community Schools)Walled Lake Consolidated Schools is considering closing one of the district’s three high schools in response to declining enrollment.At a meeting on Thursday, school board members reviewed a facilities utilization study showing the districts’ high schools were operating below their functional capacity.As a potential response to underutilization, the report studied the possibility of closing Walled Lake Central High School and consolidating students into the district's other two high schools.In a letter shared with families on Friday morning, Superintendent Michael Lonze emphasized that no final decisions have been made about the closure of facilities.The evaluation of a potential closure of Central High School, Lonze wrote, “was part of the district's broader, ongoing efforts to evaluate our facilities and ensure our learning environments are positioned to provide the strongest possible educational experiences for students.”Officials with Walled Lake Consolidated Schools declined an interview request.According to the report reviewed on Thursday, the district has seen a 24% decline in enrollment over the last 20 years. Enrollment is projected to continue declining, in line with a national trend that is driven, in part, by declining birth rates.Walled Lake’s high schools are only 52% utilized, according to the report, compared to 72% utilization of the district’s elementary and middle schools.The report said that low enrollment can lead to elective courses being cancelled, the consolidation of courses into fewer sections, and reduced opportunities for clubs and athletics. Two high schools, Walled Lake Central and Walled Lake Western, are not offering some AP courses this year due to a lack of demand.Consolidating students from three high schools down to two could alleviate those challenges and lead to more robust programming for students, according to the report. It could also save the district money: Maintaining underutilized space is more than twice as expensive as maintaining vacant space, the report said.In his letter to families, Lonze wrote that the district periodically commissions facilities utilization studies, which help the district “better understand how to maximize our resources.”But, he wrote, “We recognize that our schools are more than buildings. They are places where students learn, relationships are built, and lasting memories are made.”Underlying the district’s challenge is a gap between state funding and rising costs. This year, the district saw a 3% increase in personnel costs and 5% increase in operating costs, according to the report.But state funding, which is allocated on a per-pupil basis, only rose 2.4%. That means that even if enrollment holds steady this year, the school is in line to absorb a net loss of nearly $1 million.

articles.title: Tensions rise in Kalamazoo school district as teachers approach 100 days without a contract
articles.description: Kalamazoo Public Schools has been facing protests, student walkouts, and unfair labor practice allegations as bargaining with the local teachers’ union drags out.
articles.content: (Valentin Ivanstov / Pexels)Kalamazoo Public Schools is facing protests, student walkouts, and unfair labor practice charges in the midst of protracted collective bargaining with the local teachers union.The Kalamazoo Education Association represents more than 800 teachers, school counselors, librarians, and other workers within KPS. They negotiate a contract with the school district on a yearly basis.But bargaining has been slow: The union’s previous contract expired on August 16, nearly 100 days ago. While it’s unusual for negotiations to go on so long, this isn’t the first time they’ve gone past the expiration date of the union’s old contract.“This is the third year in a row,” said education association President Heather Reid. “It feels like a pattern.”At present, the two parties are locked in disagreements over economic issues. The union is asking for pay increases in line with the rate of inflation, which would be slightly under 4%. The school district is offering 2.11%.Representatives of the school district did not respond to a request for comment, but KPS officials have previously argued their position is justified by a need to maintain the school system’s financial health.Reid disputed this perspective. “This district has money,” she said, adding, “If we were in really bad times, our district has — or our teachers, I should say — have taken pay freezes. Throughout the years we've done what we've needed to do when things were really bad, but things aren't.”Another major source of disagreement between the union and the district is retroactive pay, a provision in the union’s old contract that required the school district to pay teachers a lump sum representing the money they would have made from raises if the contract was ratified on schedule. Kalamazoo Public Schools wants to remove this provision from the next contract.The Kalamazoo Education Association has gotten a fair amount of community support. According to MLive, students at Kalamazoo Central High School organized a walkout to support their teachers on Wednesday, despite threats of suspension and detention from school administrators.The next day, community members attended a meeting of the KPS Board of Education to express their dissatisfaction with the state of contract negotiations. Some gave public comments in support of the teachers inside the meeting. Others protested outside, bearing flashlights, glowsticks, and signs.“People want to start the year,” Reid said. “They want a fresh start, everything settled so we can focus on our students, our learning. And this is currently hanging over our heads and it's very unsettling. The teachers don't feel valued.”Frustrated with the slow pace of negotiations, KEA has filed an unfair labor practice charge against the school district, alleging bad-faith bargaining. It will be investigated by the Michigan Employment Relations Commission.While it will not be a focus of this year’s bargaining cycle, Reid said the union would like to see the school move toward multi-year contracts instead of the current system of yearly negotiations. She believes it would offer teachers more economic stability and improve relations between the union and school administrators.“Most of the districts in the county go more than one year with their contract,” Reid said. “I've seen three-year contracts, five-year contracts, two-year contracts, and going year-to-year puts us in this spot, potentially anyway, every single year. And now we're seeing it.”

articles.title: Texas says an execution went as planned. A witness says screams showed 'tremendous distress'
articles.description: Texas says an execution went as planned. A witness says screams showed 'tremendous distress' AP News Texas says an execution went as planned. A witness says screams showed ‘tremendous distress’ CNN Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour BBC Latest botched execution prompts calls for US moratorium on lethal injections The Guardian Texas Prisoner Moaned as Drugs Flowed During Execution, Wi
articles.content: A Texas official on Friday defended how the state carried out the execution of a 70-year-old man who loudly insisted he was in pain and pleaded, “Don’t let me suffer like this,” during a lethal injection that followed a struggle to find a suitable vein. Yet Reinaldo Dennes’ spiritual adviser, who had his hand on Dennes’ shoulder inside the death chamber in Huntsville, said he felt like he was holding a bucking bronco Thursday. “Twice he said, ‘It’s not working. It’s not working. It’s not going how it’s supposed to go. This isn’t right.’ Those types of words kept coming,” said the Rev. Jeff Hood, a death penalty opponent. Dennes was “clearly in tremendous distress,” said Hood, who called it torture. It was the ninth execution this year in Texas, which has a long history of using the death penalty as punishment for murder. Executions across the U.S. have garnered more attention since Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in Tennessee in September. The drug didn’t enter her bloodstream correctly. Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, said initial attempts to place two IV lines into Dennes’ hands and arms were unsuccessful. Dennes was strapped to the gurney at 6:04 p.m. Hernandez said an IV was successfully placed in the left side of his neck 16 minutes later at 6:20 p.m., followed by another line in his left foot at 6:38 p.m. Witnesses, including Hood and an Associated Press reporter, were escorted into the death chamber before Dennes began his final statement at 6:52 p.m. Lethal drugs began flowing less than a minute later, Hernandez said. Almost immediately, Dennes exclaimed: “The pain! Go! Go!” He uttered an expletive and implored “the father” to “take this pain.” He subsequently shouted: “My right leg is killing me!” and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, “I don’t think this is normal. Take me, father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.” The drugs were stopped at 7:07 p.m., and he was declared dead a minute later, slightly more than an hour after he was restrained in the death chamber, Hernandez said. “We feel that all of our processes and procedures were followed and that it was carried out as planned,” she told the AP. Hernandez said she didn’t know how many attempts were made to place IV lines. “It’s not a race — it’s not how quickly can we get this done,” she said. “It’s something you want to do correctly. There is no normal time limit. It’s what it takes for it to be successfully done.” In May, Tennessee called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers after failing for over an hour to establish an IV line. Idaho, in 2024, tried eight times to establish a line to execute Thomas Creech before stopping. Republican Gov. Brad Little subsequently signed a law making a firing squad the primary method of execution. As for Dennes’ claims of extreme pain, Hernandez said the state plans no additional inquiry. She said there were reasons to suspect he was exaggerating, adding that he complained even before the lethal drugs were given and grumbled about pain in a leg that didn’t have an IV line. Hernandez said “it makes you wonder” if the high-profile Pike case has influenced death row inmates to act out. “They watch the news. He was aware of the other executions,” Hernandez said. Dr. Paul Wax, executive director of the American College of Medical Toxicology, said he couldn’t think of any reason why an injection of pentobarbital into the left foot or left side of the neck would cause pain in the right leg. Michael Graczyk, The AP reporter who attended the execution, said witnesses can’t see when the drug starts to be administered. Dennes’ foot was covered by a sheet, and the IV in the left side of his neck wasn’t visible from their position. It’s not possible to definitively know what caused him to scream in pain. Hernandez said the lethal drugs had not passed their expiration date, though she didn’t know the date. Hood, the spiritual adviser, said assertions that Dennes was faking pain were “disgusting.” “We have heard them say repeatedly since last night that this was not botched. That is absolutely, unbelievably absurd,” Hood said. Dale Baich, an Arizona lawyer who has represented death row inmates and witnessed 17 U.S. executions, said the latest Texas lethal injection raises concerns. “Calling a prisoner’s screams an act is not a medical finding. It is an accusation, and the state should be required to produce evidence to support it,” Baich said. Associated Press reporter Kate Brumback in Atlanta contributed to this story.

articles.title: Michigan Supreme Court denies appeal on clean energy zoning rules, agrees to hear another
articles.description: The Michigan Supreme Court Friday issued a major decision involving the state’s 2023 clean energy zoning law, declining to hear an appeal from nearly 80 localities who argued that state energy regulators had acted outside their authority in their efforts to implement the new policy. In November 2024, 72 townships and seven counties filed a […]
articles.content: Stock photo/Getty ImagesThe Michigan Supreme Court Friday issued a major decision involving the state’s 2023 clean energy zoning law, declining to hear an appeal from nearly 80 localities who argued that state energy regulators had acted outside their authority in their efforts to implement the new policy. In November 2024, 72 townships and seven counties filed a challenge against the Michigan Public Service Commission, arguing the regulatory body had violated the state’s rulesmaking procedures by “unlawfully and unreasonably” redefining key terms and and creating processes and procedures “that violate the Legislature’s express and unambiguous intent.” The appeal came nearly a year after Gov. Gretchen Whitmer signed the Clean Energy and Jobs Act, Public Act 233 and 234, into law. As part of a package of clean energy bills passed by the Democratic-led Legislature, the laws gave the Michigan Public Service Commission authority over permitting renewable energy and battery storage projects above a certain size. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Public Act 233 requires energy companies and power producers to engage with localities whose clean energy permitting process matches the one put in place by the state, those companies can apply for permitting through the commission if a community fails to approve or deny the local application in a timely manner, if the local zoning process is stricter than what state law prescribes, or if a project meets the requirements laid out by the permitting law, but is denied. The Michigan Court of Appeals agreed with the localities on two points, finding that the commission had erred by only including units of government with zoning authority in its definition of an “affected local unit.” It also determined that the commission’s timeline for an affected local unit to notify a developer that they have a “compatible renewable energy ordinance” did not match the definition laid out in state law. Beyond those terms, the court largely upheld the Michigan Public Service Commission’s order implementing the law. In their appeal to the Michigan Supreme Court, the localities presented a single question: Did the Public Service Commission unlawfully and unreasonably exceed its authority in issuing all or parts of the Oct. 10 order implementing the permitting law? How Ann Arbor, Michigan, is creating its own clean energy utility While the localities argued it had, the high court denied the application for leave to appeal, “because we are not persuaded that the question presented should be reviewed by this Court.” However, the Supreme Court’s Friday order moves forward on some questions raised in a cross-appeal filed by the Michigan Public Service Commission and a collective of clean energy industry and advocacy groups. Those questions concern the Court of Appeals decision on the notification timeline and a company’s ability to move forward with a project if local elected officials do not respond to their offer to meet within 30 days, or if a meeting is never held. While the court declined to consider other questions raised by the commission and the intervenors, it instructed the Clerk of the Court to schedule oral arguments on the approved questions for January 2027. In a statement, Advanced Energy United, Clean Grid Alliance and the Michigan Energy Innovation Business Council, which intervened in the case, applauded the court’s decision to deny the local governments’ appeal, allowing the commission to move forward in implementing the permitting law. “Michigan needs to generate more energy to keep energy costs down as demand continues to surge. The Clean Energy and Jobs Act ensures business leaders have certainty to invest in Michigan, building the projects that power the state’s grid and create jobs,” Trish Demeter, senior managing director at Advanced Energy United, said in a statement. “We look forward to the Michigan Supreme Court ensuring there remains a clear, transparent statewide process that everyone can follow so we can generate the energy needed to affordably meet demand.” In a news release, Foster Swift Collins and Smith, PC, the law firm representing the local governments, noted their disappointment in the court’s decision not to hear their appeal. However, the firm also cheered its decision to uphold the Court of Appeals ruling around the definition of an “affected local unit.” “This is an important win for counties and other local governments that may not exercise zoning authority over a project site but will nevertheless experience the project’s impacts,” Michael D. Homier, the leader of Foster Swift’s municipal practice group said in a statement. “The decision confirms that those communities cannot be excluded from the rights and protections the Legislature provided under PA 233 simply because another local government exercises zoning jurisdiction.” In a statement, the Michigan Public Service Commission offered appreciation to the Supreme Court for “providing clarity on what it will review in this matter.” “We look forward to making our case,” the commission stated.

She came to Michigan seeking safety. After deportation she was killed in Venezuela.
articles.description: Fleeing violence for being trans, Q came to Michigan for a better life. But after being sexually assaulted inside a detention center, she was deported to Venezuela. Months later she was killed.
articles.content: Q came to Michigan in 2025 seeking refuge after facing violence for being trans. In 2026, she was deported to Venezuela. (Jodi Westrick / Michigan Public )In the summer of 2025, Q was looking to start a new life when she arrived in Pontiac, Michigan. Q’s niece, Rosaura Quintero, remembers feeling reassured about the possibility of Q’s new life in the United States.“Meaning confident that she was going to be much better off,” she told Michigan Public. “That she was going to have maybe the care and safety to walk peacefully down a street, work peacefully, and that nothing could happen to her — something that here in Venezuela she couldn’t do.”In Venezuela Q was viciously beaten for being transgender. She bore scars on her chest from what she said was a violent knife attack.“Here [in Venezuela] she had to stay hidden, camouflaged.. pretending,” Quintero said. “She feared for her life.”Q told Michigan Public earlier this year that she believed she was targeted because of her work through her organization, Fundación LGBTI Gente Bella. The organization’s mission was to advocate for the rights of LGBTQ+ people while also raising funds for those who needed it.Q at an event hosted by her organization, Fundación LGBTI Gente Bella, where she joined fellow hairstylists in volunteering their time and skills to provide haircuts for older adults.(Courtesy / Rosaura Quintero)“If someone passed away they helped them with the funeral — contributed to a burial or a cremation,” Quintero recalled. “They also would go to nursing homes, tidy them up, cut their (people’s) hair, groom them, they went to hospitals, meals were donated, medicines … anything someone might need that was within their means, they did it.”New church, friends, and barbershopIn Pontiac, Q started working at a local barbershop.She told Michigan Public about the day when she got a chance to prove her haircutting skills by repairing a client’s wig after another barber had botched it.“I took that wig and gave it a fabulous cut, Whitney Houston-style, something divine. I left her looking spectacular,” she said.Her budding career in hairstyling in the U.S. was cut short when she was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in February of 2026. Instead of celebrating her 50th birthday with her newfound chosen family, Q found herself in a male unit at the North Lake Detention Center in Baldwin, Michigan.At North Lake, Q was sexually assaulted over a period of several weeks. Michigan Public does not identify victims of sexual assault. When she reported the assault to police, she was examined at a hospital, transferred out of the facility, and quickly deported back to Venezuela.Restarting her life in VenezuelaQ arrived in Caracas, Venezuela, in April of this year and settled in her hometown in Barquisimeto with her sister and niece, Rosaura Quintero.“Honestly, she tried not to socialize much, not to expose herself,” she said. “Rather than suffering any harm, when she had already suffered a lot.” Q loved her three dogs, Flecha (left), Vaca (middle) and Buda (right). She often referred to them as her children. (Courtesy / Rosaura Quintero )Back at home, Quintero said, Q spent a lot of time reconnecting with her three dogs, Flecha, Vaca, and Buda — whom she often referred to as her children.“She would pick them up from the street and raise them,” Quintero saidSharing food was one of the ways Q showed her love, Quintero said. On the days the family didn’t have enough money to buy food, Q would forgo her meals so that her pups would have something to eat.“She loved to cook for us, to provide, but many times she didn't even eat, it was just for the joy of it,” she added. “She did it just for pleasure, and well, it was delicious.”According to Quintero, Q's favorite food to eat was caraotas — the Venezuelan name for black beans.“She was the one who pulled us through”For 20 years Q was a hairdresser — a career she technically began when she was around 14 years old.“She hadn't taken any courses or anything, she just practiced on my grandmother and my mother,” Quintero said. Q worked as a hairstylist for several decades and was known for her balayage. (Courtesy / Rosaura Quintero )As time went by though, Q managed, Quintero said, to become one of the best stylists in the city. She was known for her balayage — a free hand hair highlighting technique.“Whenever she told her story — it was very funny because at first, since she didn't know, they didn't pay her,” Quintero said. “She even caused some damage to some hair when she was starting out …until … years went by and she became big.”It was by cutting hair that Q managed to support her family on her income alone, Quintero said.“She was the one who pulled us through,” said Quintero. “My mom learned the hairdressing trade because of her. Nowadays, my mom is also a hairdresser, thanks to her, who always supported her.”A “fierce advocate” for trans people in Venezuela Standing up for the LGBTQ community was one of Q’s greatest passions.“She was a fierce advocate for queer people, LGBTQ people, especially trans people in Venezuela,” said Cisily Quintanilla Zuniga.Zuniga connected with Q after she was deported through the immigrant rights group No Detention Centers of Michigan.“I was a friend and an advocate and a connection to Q to amplify her story here in the U.S. and help out with support while she's in Venezuela, “ Zuniga said.Q told Michigan Public she needed to have surgery to address some of the injuries she suffered as a result of the sexual assault at North Lake. In October she managed to get that care. Q(Courtesy / Rosaura Quintero )“Today, I am healed and eager to keep working for my LGBTQ+ community. I am grateful for the work everyone does to support others. God observes everything. God sees all,” Q wrote then in a message to Michigan Public.While being back in Venezuela wasn’t easy for Q, Zuniga said she found a lot of meaning giving back to those in need.“Whatever food she had, she would take it to the hospital and try to feed people that were houseless.”Q’s dream, Zuniga said, was to open a physical space for her organization, Fundación LGBTI Gente Bella, where LGBTQ people could build community, receive support, and care.“I think her dream was to just be a trans woman, to get gender affirming surgery,” Zuniga said. “She had a strong case for asylum, she had a strong case to seek refuge in our country and to try to live a life of peace.”On November 2, 2026, Q was attacked and beaten nearly to death while attempting to make one of her regular meal deliveries to people in need, according to her niece.Quintero said she usually would accompany her aunt on these runs but wasn't able to that day. She remembers Q telling her that she didn’t care if she went alone, she just wanted to help.“If she didn't go make that donation, that food was going to go to waste. With so many people hungry, she was never going to allow that.”Documentation from the hospital provided to Michigan Public by Q’s family states Q received multiple blows to the head and body leading to a severe traumatic brain injury.Eleven days after the attack, Q’s family made the difficult decision to take her off life support. Q died on November 13 at the intensive care unit of the Hospital Central Universitario "Dr. Antonio María Pineda" in Barquisimeto, Venezuela. She was born in Caracas but spent the majority of her life in Barquisimeto. She was 50 years old. Q(Courtesy / Q)“I lost the most important person in my life. The only person I could count on for everything,” Quintero said. “But I also feel proud for who she was and wherever she may be I will always be thankful for everything that she did with love and everything she gave with love for me.”Q is remembered by her family and friends both in Venezuela and Michigan for her optimism, her relentless spirit, and her determination to make the world a better place.“In another life, I would choose her again … without hesitation as my aunt, as my mother, as my unconditional friend,” Quintero said. “I would never change her.”Cisily Quintanilla Zuniga said No Detention Centers of Michigan is raising funds to help Q’s family pay for funeral expenses.

articles.title: Warren driver sentenced for leaving scene of injury accident
articles.content: A 51-year-old Warren man was recently sentenced to two years probation after pleading no contest to a charge of leaving the scene of a fatal or serious-injury accident for striking a man with the vehicle he was driving in 2024, according to court records. Tony Prather received the sentence Nov. 12 from Macomb County Circuit Judge Jennifer Faunce in Mount Clemens after entering the plea in September, records say. Prather was granted status under a law that defers a one-year jail term and allows the 5-year felony to be reduced to a 4-year felony, assault with a dangerous weapon, if he complies with conditions until a November 2027 review, records say. Prather spent 55 days in jail. A second charge of driving with a suspended license causing serious injury and Prather’s habitual status were dismissed. His driver’s license also has been suspended by the Michigan Secretary of State, and Prather was ordered to pay $1,455 in restitution to Macomb County, records say. Prather and his male passenger left a bar and were riding in Prather’s truck on Feb. 23, 2024, and Prather was dropping him off at a residence, prosecutors said. Prather struck him with his vehicle and left the scene with the victim lying in the road, according to authorities. Prather was initially charged with attempted murder, but it was dismissed.

The order released today granted AT&T's request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC's previous approval of AT&T's petition to discontinue service. articles.title: Video: Mayor Mamdani Injured After Soccer Game
articles.content: NEW YORK (VINnews) — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani tore his Achilles tendon during a friendly indoor soccer game against members of the city’s press corps Thursday night, leaving him on crutches and wearing a protective walking boot. The 35-year-old mayor revealed the injury Friday morning at a City Hall news conference, where he appeared on crutches while discussing his administration’s plan to close Rikers Island. Mayor Zohran Mamdani says he tore his achilles playing a friendly game of soccer with the press and will be in a boot for 6-8 weeks. MORE: https://t.co/8lZY7d9J8L https://t.co/ieRUtZGvB4 — Henry Rosoff (@HenryRosoff) November 20, 2026 Mamdani said the injury occurred during the second half of the match while he was running for the ball. It was a non-contact injury, and the mayor acknowledged that he had not stretched before taking the field. “I did not stretch,” Mamdani said, explaining how the injury happened. The mayor also joked about his age, saying he scored shortly after entering the game before suffering the injury. “I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch and I forgot that I was 35,” Mamdani said. Despite the injury, Mamdani said his team, made up of members of the mayor’s office, defeated the press corps 10-5. The mayor said he expects to wear a walking boot for six to eight weeks and anticipates being able to return to playing soccer in approximately nine months. The injury did not prevent Mamdani from appearing at Friday’s announcement, although he required crutches and a protective boot. The soccer match was a friendly competition between the mayor’s staff and members of the New York City press corps, offering an unusual opportunity for reporters who regularly cover City Hall to face the administration on the playing field. For now, the mayor will have to trade the soccer field for a lengthy recovery period.

articles.title: Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button
articles.description: Google search is making it even easier to access AI tools on the search page.
articles.content: Google's flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that's been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely. Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There's an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The "I'm Feeling Lucky" button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone. The search button has obviously been a part of Google's search page forever. However, it wasn't in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Detroit police restore oversight board’s footage access. But why was it taken away?
articles.description: The board has argued that the restrictions impaired BOPC’s ability to carry out its charter-mandated duties and slowed the work of its investigative arm, which has grappled for years with a citizen complaint backlog.
articles.content: Detroit’s police oversight board has regained direct access to police camera footage after months of relying on the discretion of the department it’s meant to hold accountable. Investigators with Detroit’s Board of Police Commissioners can once again directly access raw police camera footage after the Detroit Police Department stripped BOPC’s full access to body and dashboard camera recordings and certain records on May 15. Since then, the board — which is responsible for independent civilian oversight of DPD — had to rely on partially redacted footage, records and reports from the police department. Prior to the process change in the spring, the BOPC investigators had been able to independently access a slew of DPD records since the board’s establishment in 1974. Detroit Police Chief Todd Bettison was responsible for revoking — and, recently, restoring — access. But, between police commissioners, their investigators, the city’s top attorney Conrad Mallett and Bettison himself, confusion persists over why access was restricted to begin with. The board has argued that the restrictions impaired BOPC’s ability to carry out its charter-mandated duties and slowed the work of its investigative arm, which has grappled for years with a citizen complaint backlog. There are currently more than 2,000 open complaints, according to the board’s Police Accountability Dashboard. It was not immediately clear exactly how many reports were delayed due to the May process change. The BOPC’s Office of the Chief Investigator, led by Jerome Warfield, investigates non-criminal citizen complaints against the Detroit Police Department. Warfield served on the board from 2009 to 2013, and has been the chief investigator since 2023. During that time, Warfield told BridgeDetroit, there has never been a leak from the office, nor has the OCI been accused of “infringing upon the privilege that we have of using sensitive information to do our investigation.” “Imagine, if you will, the prosecutor had to go to the perpetrator and said, ‘Could you send me some proof that you did the crime that you are accused of doing?’” said Warfield, calling the process of restricting BOPC access a “muddled mess.” “That’s how ludicrous this is to me; that we’re asking the ones who are being accused to send us evidence that they are in control of,” he said. Previously, OCI investigators could log in via a computer or use a cellphone app to directly access raw data or footage. The spring process change meant investigators had to request certain DPD footage and that sensitive data was redacted by DPD officers before it was turned over. Bettison said that he ultimately made the decision to restore BOPC’s access after receiving conflicting guidance about who had authority over the process. “Then, it was told to me that I had the decision, and it was on me whether or not I would restore it or not,” Bettison told commissioners at Thursday’s meeting. “And so, if the power is mine to restore it, when I was told it wasn’t mine initially, then I restored it.” Bettison did not explicitly say where his initial direction came from. The chief declined BridgeDetroit’s request to comment following the meeting. According to Warfield and a June statement from board commissioners, the BOPC was told direct access to footage had to end due to compliance issues with FBI policies for handling sensitive criminal justice and public safety information. These rules are set forth by the bureau’s Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division, a criminal justice “hub” that manages databases where the records are stored. The sensitive information — often referred to as “CJIS data,” — can be included in records found in the databases that the OCI has historically had direct access to. Police camera footage, for example, is sometimes roped in because it can capture things like police computer terminals, which can sometimes contain CJIS data. Police commissioners said in the June statement that they felt the push was coming from the FBI, in conjunction with the Michigan Commission on Law Enforcement Standards, or MCOLES, housed within the Michigan State Police Department. This was based on a private May 4 virtual meeting commissioners and Warfield have said was attended by representatives from MSP, MCOLES and the FBI. Agencies found to be noncompliant with CJIS Security Policy are subject to “restriction, suspension, or termination of CJIS access,” according to the board’s statement. Warfield and several police commissioners have said Bettison has been very supportive of maintaining BOPC’s full access to police footage and records since May. Warfield reiterated at Thursday’s meeting that Bettison tried on multiple occasions during the May 4 meeting to work with the FBI and state agencies on proposals that would maintain access — all of which were shot down by the federal and state law enforcement officials, according to Warfield and the commissioners. According to a Thursday statement from the FBI, its officials attended the May meeting at the request of MSP, the body responsible for administering statewide use of CJIS programs and enforcing the rules. “However, the FBI did not direct or make decisions regarding the Detroit Board of Police Commissioners access to body cam footage as the matter falls outside the scope of the FBI’s CJIS Division,” the emailed statement to BridgeDetroit notes. In a Friday statement emailed to BridgeDetroit, MSP also confirmed it was not responsible for the decision to strip BOPC of direct access. Although, MSP said it has been “consistent in its stance” for “many years” that BOPC and OCI are not eligible for access to CJIS systems and the data that they hold. BOPC, the statement notes, is considered a non-criminal justice entity, and its Charter-based “oversight” capacity, “is not a criminal justice function according to state and federal law.” Because DPD is the authorized agency for the records and databases, MSP adds, it’s DPD’s responsibility to ensure that data is not unlawfully disseminated. Warfield said at Thursday’s meeting that OCI investigators’ requests had never been strictly denied by DPD. But the change slowed investigations, often requiring multiple rounds of communication between investigators and the officers responsible for fulfilling their requests. On some occasions, Warfield said, investigators were told footage was not available and later found out that it had been. He also told BridgeDetroit that in addition to being fingerprinted and undergoing extensive background checks upon hiring, OCI investigators are “CJIS-certified.” “It seems like we were bamboozled at the end of the day,” said Warfield. “So it’s hard to say, and no one wants to take responsibility.” When BridgeDetroit asked about the OCI investigators’ CJIS-certified status, an MSP public information officer referred back to the original statement. MCOLES Executive Director Tim Bourgeois said in a Friday statement that MCOLES has “no statutory authority over the topic at hand,” and took no part in the process. Restored access doesn’t resolve broader concerns Despite some restored access, the OCI still lacks direct access to multiple systems and reports it previously had, Warfield said Thursday. It’s unclear how, when or whether that access will be restored. Commissioners are also concerned that nothing is in place to prevent access from being stripped again in the future. District 3 Commissioner Darious Morris, who was not at Thursday’s meeting, previously told BridgeDetroit that the access restrictions undermined civilian oversight, which “kills transparency” and weakens the ability to hold people accountable. “We need the information to know what’s going on and to be able to root out misconduct and move them toward accountability,” he said. “So it (restricting access to information) was like taking the legs from up under us.” Still, some commissioners and community members view the restored camera footage access as a significant, if partial, victory. “Certainly I’m relieved that some of that access has been restored,” District 7 Commissioner Victoria Camille, who has been one of the most publicly outspoken commissioners on the issue, said at Thursday’s meeting. “…We should continue to advocate for the remainder of that access to be restored, and for whatever necessary reforms have to happen at the state and federal level to ensure that threats like this don’t prevail, even temporarily, for any other civilian oversight agency,” she said. Warfield told BridgeDetroit Thursday that looking back, “we should have fought,” when direct access was revoked. During Thursday’s meeting, Warfield said more formal paperwork might be needed in the future to ensure “this doesn’t happen again.” Mallett previously raised the possible need for similar agreements when discussing the restoration of OCI access. Frequent BOPC meeting attendee Eric Blount, Minister at Sacred Heart Catholic Church, told BridgeDetroit his trust in DPD and the other involved agencies has been impacted by the “smoke and mirrors” that allowed access to be revoked in the first place. “You don’t know what to believe, and therefore, how can you trust them?” Blount said “…When you lose trust, you begin to question everything.”

articles.content: The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs medical campus in Rapid City, South Dakota. (Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)WASHINGTON — Many military veterans are opposing a U.S. House-passed proposal to revamp retirement and disability benefits, saying it threatens future veterans’ compensation. The House passed two bills last week that address the issue. What’s at stake is whether some 58,000 — and counting — medically retired veterans who suffered combat-related injuries before meeting 20 years of service can receive both full disability and full retirement, and who pays for it. Under current law those medically retired before reaching the 20-year mark do not receive full retirement. The standalone Major Richard Star Act, which would provide full disability and retirement benefits to veterans who were injured in combat before reaching 20 years of service, passed Nov. 12 in an overwhelming 392-18 vote. The other measure, a package that combined 60 pieces of veterans-related legislation, passed by voice vote a day earlier, on Veterans Day. That package, titled the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, or TCAVA, includes the Major Richard Star Act. While the Major Richard Star Act contains no provision for funding the benefits increase, the TCAVA does in the form of cutting future disability support for sleep apnea and tinnitus, as well as raising funding fees on VA home loans. Sleep apnea and tinnitus are common injuries among veterans who are exposed to repeated loud noises and poor sleep conditions. Tinnitus, or persistent ringing and buzzing when no sound is present, ranked first among all disability compensation recipients in 2025, according to the Veteran Benefits Administration’s annual report. The TCAVA also combines dozens of provisions meant to streamline some VA infrastructure and health professional credentialing, as well as expand benefits for caregivers and survivors, including allowing survivors who remarry before age 55 to continue to be eligible for benefits, among other measures. The Major Richard Star Act would cost $13 billion over the next decade, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. The budget office does not have an estimate for TCAVA. The Senate is only in session for four more weeks in the 119th Congress, and it’s unclear if the Republican-led Senate will take up either bill for a vote. An aide in the office of Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said leadership does not have an update on the bills at this time. Future cuts? Several veterans have spoken out against TCAVA, expressing concern that future veterans will have to pay for retirement and disability benefits that current veterans should be entitled to in full. “That’s a problem I have, and my daughter just joined the Marines recently. If that passes, that takes away possible disability benefits from her in the future, if something were to happen to her,” combat U.S. Army veteran Matt Inscho, 44, told States Newsroom in an interview Thursday. Inscho, who lives in Indiana, Pennsylvania, deployed twice to Afghanistan and Iraq over six-and-a-half years until he medically retired after suffering migraines and blackouts. His main duties included repairing military aircraft. States Newsroom received numerous emails from veterans unhappy with the TCAVA. Veterans service organizations, including DAV: Disabled American Veterans and the VFW, have also spoken out against TCAVA, particularly taking issue that the Republican-controlled House passed the bill by voice vote on Veteran’s Day. “On a day when America honors the brave men and women who stepped forward to defend our freedom, House leaders chose to sneak through legislation threatening earned benefits for millions of veterans, their families and survivors,” said DAV National Commander John Donovan in a written statement after the vote. “If Members of Congress believe these cuts are justified, they should have the courage and integrity to put their names on the record and defend them to the veterans they represent,” he added. House Speaker Mike Johnson’s office did not respond to a States Newsroom request for comment. The American Legion, which supports both bills, said claims that TCAVA would cut future benefits is “not quite the story.” Issuing new rules to overhaul disability categories “has been something that the VA has been working on,” American Legion’s deputy legislative director, Bailey Bishop, told States Newsroom Friday. “There is a specific protection written into (TCAVA) that says that VA may not use this new rating system … as an excuse to go back and pull veterans who have already been rated for these conditions and look at them again,” Bishop said. The legion has also praised the proposal for combining dozens of bills that will affect more than 32 million veterans and family members, according to the organization. “At the end of the day, we want to do the most amount of good and reach the most amount of people,” Bishop said. Democratic discharge petition Rep. Mark Takano of California, the top Democrat on the House Veterans Affairs Committee, filed a discharge petition in May to bypass leadership and bring the standalone Major Richard Star Act to the floor for a vote. Republican Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina became the 218th signature — the number required this Congress to trigger a vote — on the petition in September, just before the midterm recess. Other Republicans who signed the petition included Reps. Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Jason Van Drew of New Jersey and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The bill overwhelmingly passed on Nov. 12, with only 18 Republicans in opposition, the majority of whom belong to the House Freedom Caucus, which sometimes opposes government spending. Rep. Tim Burchett, a Tennessee Republican, recorded and posted a video on social media as he was leaving the U.S. House after voting against the bill. “The Democrats, as you remember yesterday, messed up, and so now they’re trying to pull the Richard Star bill back, and so they can pass it again,” Burchett said, referring to Democrats’ failure to force a roll-call vote on TCAVA the previous day. “But theirs does not have a pay-for, so it just adds to the $40 trillion in debt, and that’s a terrible way to run government.” Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., praised the bipartisan passage of the Major Richard Star Act, crediting Takano’s discharge petition for “clearing the way for a vote.” “For months, the legislation stalled in the House amid disagreements over its cost among House Republican leaders. Instead, they passed legislation that would create the largest cut to veterans’ benefits in history,” he said in a statement referring to the GOP-led voice vote passing TCAVA on Veterans’ Day. The Major Richard Star Act was introduced in March 2025 of this Congress with Republican Rep. Gus Bilirakis of Florida as the main sponsor. The TCAVA was introduced in June 2026 by Republican Rep. Mike Bost of Illinois. Major Richard Star was a combat veteran who developed lung cancer after burn pit exposure and who advocated for disabled veterans until his death in 2021.

articles.title: TWTS: From 'dead beat' to 'deadbeat'
articles.description: When we’re tired, we might be dead beat, which is different from saying we’re deadbeats.
articles.content: “Deadbeat” can describe someone who’s exhausted and ready to collapse, or someone who’s irresponsible, unreliable, and maybe even a little shady. The word has taken on some pretty different meanings over the years, depending on whether you're describing how you feel after a long day or someone who owes you money.The word "beat," meaning tired or exhausted, dates back to the early 1800s. Add "dead" as an intensifier, as in “dead certain,” and you get "dead beat." One of the earliest recorded uses, from 1811, described a boxer who had been beaten so badly, he was left lying on the ground, dead beat.Over time, "beat" picked up other meanings, including cheating, taking advantage of someone, and being irresponsible or disreputable. By the Civil War era, deadbeat was being used to describe a lazy or unreliable person, particularly someone who couldn't or wouldn't repay debts. Eventually, the term became a noun for the person themselves.Today, "deadbeat" can carry some serious weight, especially when describing an absent or irresponsible parent. But it can also be used much more casually, as a joking way to describe someone who, for example, keeps forgetting to return a library book or return a call to a friend. The difference between a deadbeat dad and a deadbeat library patron is considerable, though neither is likely to be winning any awards for responsibility.For more on the history and changing meaning of "deadbeat," listen to the audio above.

Democrats see missed opportunities after Black turnout surge across the South
articles.description: As new details emerge about a Black midterm voting surge in Southern states, missed opportunities for Democrats are coming under more scrutiny, such as close U.S. Senate races in Florida and Louisiana that might have added to the party’s advantage in Washington, D.C. Democrats in both states nominated Black candidates for U.S. Senate and turnout […]
articles.content: Florida U.S. Senate Democratic candidate Angie Nixon talks to reporters following her concession speech earlier this month. Some experts point to her narrow loss, and another in Louisiana, as evidence that more funding could produce even better Senate results in 2028. (Photo by Christine Sexton/ Florida Phoenix)As new details emerge about a Black midterm voting surge in Southern states, missed opportunities for Democrats are coming under more scrutiny, such as close U.S. Senate races in Florida and Louisiana that might have added to the party’s advantage in Washington, D.C. Democrats in both states nominated Black candidates for U.S. Senate and turnout among Black voters was high. Looking back, some political analysts see lessons for Democrats looking ahead to 2028, noting that more money from national party committees could have notched them at least two more wins. In Mississippi, of Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom saw an unexpected and historic success and will become the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. Similar bumps from Black voters in Florida and Louisiana that might have helped Democrats had there been more help, observers say. “Louisiana is definitely the one the Democrats let slip away,” said Robert Collins, a political analyst and professor at Dillard University in New Orleans. In Louisiana, Republican Julia Letlow, an incumbent U.S. House member, won a narrow victory of about 25,000 votes over Democrat Jamie Davis, a farmer in the rural Delta region, for an open U.S. Senate seat. Democratic strategist Matt McDermott said that in Florida, Democrat Angie Nixon was “underfunded” in a 2.9-point loss to Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody. Immediately after the election, Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried called out her national party for not sending money earlier to her state’s candidates. “Florida Democrats are looking at the results across the country and can only imagine what kind of a day we would be having if we had sustained national support and the investment this state deserves,” Fried said in a conference call with reporters after Election Day. “It is not about spending in Florida. It is about investing early in Florida the infrastructure that is necessary to win the third-largest state.” Louisiana was not on McDermott’s list of states most vulnerable to Senate flips in 2028, but he told Stateline it’s “certainly a state where Democrats could play” even though incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. John Kennedy would be a formidable foe. In Louisiana, Letlow had a huge fundraising advantage, including almost $3 million in super PAC money compared with only a little less than $130,000 in such funds for Davis, Collins said. Davis also had little statewide name recognition as a municipal official in rural Tensas Parish, unlike Mississippi’s Colom, who was a well-known sitting district attorney with competitive fundraising and super PAC support. “Despite all those disadvantages, Davis came within 1.8 points,” Collins noted. “If the Democratic National Committee had put a couple million dollars into the race, on television ads and get-out-the-vote efforts, Davis wins this race, and I think he wins easily.” The DNC referred comment to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which sets spending priorities for U.S. Senate races. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Louisiana Democrats’ near-miss on Senate seat gives party hope for governor’s race Data scientist Lenny Bronner pointed out the Louisiana near miss in an analysis this month of Black turnout in Southern states for states that had released detailed results. The South has most of the nation’s Black population, 59% as of last year, according to U.S. Census Bureau estimates reviewed by Stateline. “Worth wondering, for Democrats, what could have happened in Louisiana if they had had Mississippi style turnout among Black voters,” Bronner wrote in an X post. Bronner’s analysis for Arkansas, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina and Virginia showed that precincts with large Black populations had higher turnout, compared with 2024, than areas with less Black population. The difference was especially stark for both Louisiana and Mississippi, indicating that Black voters were particularly motivated to vote this year compared to other groups. However, Louisiana’s most heavily Black precincts only reached about 80% of 2024 turnout, when Donald Trump faced off against then-Vice President Kamala Harris, while similar precincts in Mississippi were near 100% of 2024 turnout. Democrat Colom’s Senate victory in Mississippi was historic, the first for a popularly elected Black senator from the state (there were previous Black senators after the Civil War when the legislature elected senators) and the first Democrat since 1982. Keneshia Grant, an associate professor at Howard University who wrote a 2020 book on Black Americans’ effect on the Democratic party in the South, said Black voters have long had power in Mississippi even if they were voting for Republicans willing to seek their vote. This may have been the first time they saw a realistic chance for a Democrat. Moody defeats Nixon in US Senate race “Black voter turnout could have increased because they believed it would truly matter this go-round,” Grant said. “They are very clear about what is and isn’t possible in their state.” In Florida, NBC exit polling found strong support for Nixon, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, among Black voters: 94% of Black women and 77% of Black men voted for Nixon. “As a Black woman, I will stand for my vote,” Saretta Weston, a 35-year-old accountant, said after casting her ballot in Leon County, Florida. “There’s been a lot of oppression in (the) past. As of right now we have the opportunity to do that, what many before us could not do.” North Carolina elected Democrats to 11 of 14 U.S. House seats, including seven flips. There was a U.S. Senate flip in South Carolina, and Georgia elected its first Black and first woman governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms. Even in Arkansas, where Republicans swept statewide races, Democrats flipped 10 state House seats, enough to break a Republican supermajority and give Democrats a voice in budget votes. The narrow defeat for a Democratic challenger in Louisiana’s U.S. Senate race gave Democrats hope for statewide races next year, with a chance that Davis might run for governor next year. Davis did not return an e-mail requesting comment. He told The Guardian in an interview published Thursday that it “stings to come close” — he lost by less than 2 percentage points — and said that he did not have enough money to fight damaging attack ads from Republicans. And in an interview before the election, Democratic consultant James Carville noted the lack of national party funding support and told the Louisiana Illuminator, “If Jamie loses by two points, we are going to get up Wednesday morning, and we are going to wonder where the hell were you (national Democrats)?” Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein contributed to this report. Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org. Judge refuses to dismiss Alex Murdaugh’s original indictments in killings of his wife and son
articles.description: Judge refuses to dismiss Alex Murdaugh’s original indictments in killings of his wife and son AP News Judge denies Alex Murdaugh's bid to dismiss murder charges ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Judge rejects request by Murdaugh lawyers to throw out indictments WYFF Judge denies motion to dismiss Murdaugh’s indictments, Sumter County trial remains scheduled WIS News 10 Judge rejects Alex Murdaugh's pus
articles.content: COLUMBIA S.C. (AP) — A South Carolina judge on Friday refused to dismiss the original murder indictments against Alex Murdaugh in the killings of his wife and son. Judge Debra McCaslin’s ruling came after a hearing on Nov. 13, when Murdaugh’s attorneys argued for nearly an hour that the chief investigator lied to a Colleton County grand jury in 2022 about blood spatter being found on Murdaugh’s T-shirt. Prosecutors say they have plenty of evidence supporting the charges. The ruling clears the way for the disgraced lawyer’s April retrial on the murder charges. The South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence in May, ruling a court clerk improperly influenced jurors during his 2023 trial. The chief investigator in the case, former State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen, was central to Murdaugh’s arguments. McCaslin wrote in her order that any mistakes by Owen were not intentional and that other evidence was enough to support the indictments. Still, she said she was disappointed that Owen failed to read a report saying there wasn’t blood on the T-shirt before making his presentation to the grand jury. “Law enforcement bears a fundamental duty to thoroughly review and accurately represent the complete evidentiary record,” the judge wrote. “Oversights of this nature undermine public confidence in the integrity of the criminal justice system.” Any issues about inconsistencies in evidence are matters for the trial and cross examination, McCaslin said. Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients, and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer. Defense lawyer Jim Griffin said at the Nov. 13 hearing that when prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial. The false claim about the blood spatter was the only thing anyone heard that could link him to the place and time of the killings, Griffin said. “A phone call doesn’t put him there. The video doesn’t put him there,” Griffin said. “The blood from his murdered son sprang through the air -- it’s raining back on him -- puts him there.” Owen also told grand jurors that the same ammunition load of buckshot in one chamber and large birdshot in the other used to kill Paul Murdaugh was found loaded in weapons all over the Murdaugh property. This was not the case. Prosecutors wrote that “a single mistake is not bad faith” and that other evidence supports the charges. Owen, who abruptly retired in 2024, told grand jurors about the video Paul Murdaugh recorded in which Alex Murdaugh’s voice could be heard at the scene, contradicting his denials. Owen also told them about the family’s mounting debts and how Murdaugh’s schemes to steal from clients and his law firm were close to being discovered. Prosecutors said Murdaugh killed his wife and son because he thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to cover up his thefts.

articles.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
articles.description: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn't stay private.
articles.content: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.Read full article Comments

articles.content: YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens. The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first “bellwether” trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was supposed to start in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court. The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California, judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants. Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. It also agreed to implement stricter safeguards for teens, but is pushing TikTok and YouTube to do the same. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.

articles.title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
articles.description: A recent brightening turned out to be from a star orbiting inside another.
articles.content: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act. In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.” Shared envelopes Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.Read full article Comments
