articles.title: Jeremy Moss: We need to reassert Congressional authority, put Trump in check
articles.description: Rep.-Elect Jeremy Moss speaks with Stateside's April Baer about the "big and bold" things he hopes the Democratic majority accomplish in affordability, foreign policy, and healthcare.
articles.content: Senator Jeremy Moss (D-Southfield) chairs the Senate Elections and Ethics Committee. He says Michigan has some of the weakest ethics standards in the country for elected officials.(Rick Pluta / Michigan Public Radio Network )Democratic state Senator Jeremy Moss beat Troy mayor Ethan Baker in the race for Michigan's 11th Congressional District. Moss will represent Oakland County communities including Pontiac, Farmington Hills, and Royal Oak. The seat was open after being vacated by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens.Moss believes he represents a "new generation of leadership" in national politics."We said all along, and it got a rise out of people that the Democratic Party could no longer be the party that shows up to the knife fight carrying a pie chart," Moss said to Stateside's April Baer. "And so we need to throw a punch that's a little stronger, that's a little tougher, and that meets this moment to do big and bold things."Those big and bold moves include reasserting Congressional authority on tariffs and war powers, Moss said. "Donald Trump's reckless and dangerous and visionless foreign policy has had real impacts abroad both for civilians and our service members," Moss said. "But we're also paying for it at the gas pump. So Congress has to be a co-equal branch of government."As Moss begins his term, he'll also make history as Michigan's first openly gay Congressional member. "You have to be in the places and the rooms where decisions about your life, your livelihoods, your futures are being made," he said. "We have to pass the Equality Act ... We have to stand up to this shameful and harmful rhetoric that attacks the most vulnerable people in our community."Scroll up to hear the full conversation, or read the interview transcript below.Full interview with Jeremy MossApril Baer: What was this campaign like for you?Jeremy Moss: Intense at times. Rewarding in the end. But gratifying. I really feel like the election results portray exactly what Michiganders are feeling: fed up with the chaos and corruption coming out of Washington, aggravated by the squeeze at the grocery store, the squeeze at the gas pump, and ready for change. So, we held on to our safer Democratic seat here in Oakland County, but we flipped three seats from red to blue around the state, and helped deliver this historic Democratic majority that's ready to roll up our sleeves and get things done.AB: I want to talk more about your plans for the incoming Congressional session, but I did want to ask, you are going to be occupying the seat that is currently held by Haley Stevens, who made a rather spectacular break with a lot of opinion within the Democratic Party - in crossing over to endorse Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate race. I know this is outside of you and your campaign and what you were working on, but I wonder if you have any insight into how her reversal has been received throughout the 11th?JM: Obviously, these were choices that she decided to make that I strongly disagreed with. I think we can have internal debates as Democrats about the direction of our party, the tone and rhetoric, ensuring that everybody who is left of center can feel comfortable and safe, included in the big tent of our Democratic Party. But in no way, shape or form do I believe that the Republicans, led by Donald Trump, which Mike Rogers was following right along, is the solution to our problems here. I believe that the challenges that we're facing, the corruption, the cruelty of ICE, the stripping away of our rights, can only be met right now by an incoming Democratic majority. And that meant we needed to have a Democratic majority in the House, which I'm entering. And yes, a Democratic majority in the Senate. And the voters spoke, and Abdul El-Sayed and I are going to work together to take on these big challenges for Michigan. And it was a total rebuke of anybody who wanted to continue to follow these MAGA set of politics. And I hope it's a wake-up call for Republicans, because Mike Rogers had the opportunity to present himself as a Mitt Romney or John McCain type of figure. But he didn't. He was stumping with Donald Trump, and JD Vance, and Robert Kennedy - some of the most abhorrent figures of our time. And that is not worthy of any sort of political support.AB: Jeremy, some people have interpreted the Democrats big wins in this election as a mandate for big changes in Washington. First of all, do you share that view?JM: Oh, yeah. No, no question about it. And that's what we campaigned on, too. I represent a new generation of leadership, and I think that is sorely needed in our politics, in our party, in representation, in Congress, in Washington, D.C.But I was also stumping for a stronger and tougher and bolder Democratic Party. We said all along, and it got a rise out of people that the Democratic Party could no longer be the party that shows up to the knife fight carrying a pie chart. And so we need to throw a punch that's a little stronger, that's a little tougher, and that meets this moment to do big and bold things. I think about us flipping the state Senate for the first time in 40 years in 2022. And I became president (pro tempore) of the Michigan State Senate, and we wasted no time passing some big, generational, monumental pieces of policy that languished for 40 years: the first gun safety laws in a generation, scrapping our 1931 abortion felony, putting LGBTQ rights in our state's civil rights law. And voters rewarded that by increasing our Democratic majority in the Michigan Senate this last time around. So the only way that we're going to be able to build trust with voters is if we do the things they elected us to do. And I think it has to be bold action on lowering costs and bold action on taking on corruption in Washington.AB: So what does that bold view mean in terms of the economic needs that Democrats hope to meet? What do you hope to do with other members of the caucus to try to lower costs?JM: So we have to reassert Congressional authority. Congressional authority under MAGA leadership has just bowed to the feet of Donald Trump and has been a weak branch of government. And that's no good for for the people of this country when you have an executive that does whatever he wants, and Congress is too weak and cowardly to put a check on what's going on. So this includes a check on tariffs. Congress should be setting tariff policy, and not the president. And so no place has felt more pain due to these trade wars than the state of Michigan, especially with regards to Canada. Canada is our ally. Canada is our friend. We go back and forth with trade across our borders. And it's impacted us back at home with tariffs, and retaliatory tariffs that we're paying for when we shop for everyday goods. We also have to reassert congressional authority on war powers. Donald Trump's reckless, and dangerous, and visionless foreign policy has had real impacts abroad, both for civilians and our service members. But we're also paying for it at the gas pump. So Congress has to be a co-equal branch of government that puts a check on the most corrupt and and dangerous decisions coming out of Donald Trump's administration.AB: Let's talk about health care. Medicare for All was the banner that Abdul El-Sayed campaigned on, and I wonder if something like that falls under what you view as bold action on health care right now? Is that something that you would be willing to get behind?JM: I think we have to get to a place where there's universal health care coverage in this country. And nobody should go bankrupt trying to pay medical bills, and nobody should be denied coverage if they have an emergency or a systemic problem.I think the best way to get there first is with a public option, and ensuring that if you don't have that social safety net, if you don't have that coverage through your job, you can tap into public option health care that's provided by the government. But I would love to see which plans for expanding Medicare are the most viable to get the most amount of coverage, and to make sure that we can have universal care in this country.AB: You talked a little bit about foreign policy, and it's clear that has been something that's been on a lot of voters minds. I was thinking back to a conversation that you and I had several years ago, when you were still in the state legislature, and we were talking about support for Israel. At that time, you mentioned that you felt like the term "Zionist" was one that you could readily embrace, and you also talked about what Zionism means to you. But I'm just wondering where you see that relationship now that you're entering the DC landscape?JM: Yeah, and I think I said then, and I would stand by this today, that Zionist as a word, has just been co-opted as as a slur against people who support Israel's existence. I say this all the time: Israel has a 40-year peace treaty with Egypt. Israel has a 30-year peace treaty with Jordan. That's that's the core of, I guess, what Zionism really is, in my purview. That Israel has a right to exist. It has a right to secure and safe borders. None of that could defeat the goals and aspirations for a secure, safe, and peace-seeking Palestinian state. I am supportive of a two state solution where a Palestinian state, an Israeli state, can live side by side, can have peaceful governments recognizing each other, and brokering a peace with one another, and agreeing on the borders. That's what Israel has done with Jordan. That's what Israel has done with Egypt. And I want to figure out, how do we chart the path for Israel and a Palestinian state to have the same type of future so that both people can live in the region peaceably, safely, securely, and with self-determination?AB: Jeremy, you were part of a pretty big civil rights moment this year. Michigan has never had an openly gay, LGBTQ member of of the House before. Did this feel like a big achievement as far as you were concerned?JM: Yeah, it's kind of been a long journey along the way. I think about my time running for the state legislature 12 years ago. And the hot topic was, were we going to amend our state's civil rights law? That now seems like passe. Of course, we should protect people in their workplace, at home, in healthcare, in education, from having the full access to utilize services in Michigan and not be discriminated against because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. But it took 50 years from the signing of our Civil Rights Act until we passed the law that put LGBTQ rights in that act with the bill that I sponsored into law back in 2023. So, you know, you have to be in the places and the rooms where decisions about your life, your livelihoods, your futures are being made. And so for the very first time, we're going to have an LGBTQ voice from Michigan in Congress. We have to pass the Equality Act - that's the federal version of our state's civil rights law. We have to stand up to this shameful and harmful rhetoric that attacks the most vulnerable people in our community. People wanted to run yet another campaign on the backs of trans people. I have said this: I do not know a family in my district that sits at the dinner table really lamenting about the trans athlete. It's just absolutely ridiculous that somehow this became an oversized political issue when people were talking about prescription drug costs, healthcare costs, gas prices, grocery prices. And somehow MAGA wanted to make it all about trans people and their lives and their futures. We got to make sure this community is protected under the law.AB: Jeremy Moss is the new representative-elect for Michigan's 11th district. Jeremy, thank you so much for your time. Good luck in D.C..JM: Thank you very much.

articles.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump will likely veto many of the bills that Democrats pass once they take control of Congress next year, he said Friday, though he suggested negotiations on healthcare and immigration were possible. “They’re going to send things my way and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send […]
articles.content: President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on August 6, 2026. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump will likely veto many of the bills that Democrats pass once they take control of Congress next year, he said Friday, though he suggested negotiations on healthcare and immigration were possible. “They’re going to send things my way and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send more things and I’m going to veto them,” he said. “But I think after a month or so, they’re going to send things, and I’m going to say, ‘I’m going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’” Trump then referred to House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, both of New York, as “smart” and indicated he would be willing to work with them on some issues. “There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare. I am open to great healthcare,” he said. “Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.” Trump said several Democrats have called him in recent weeks, including Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who he said wanted to discuss border security. “I received a phone call two days ago from the new governor-elect of Texas. She was really nice. It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border,” he said. “And I think we’ll be able to work something out because that’s a very important thing.” Must-pass items Trump and Democratic leaders in Congress will need to negotiate much more than healthcare and immigration once divided government begins in January. They will need to work out bipartisan agreement on the dozen annual government spending bills that fund scores of departments and agencies as well as the thousands of programs they administer. Failing to accomplish the work, or approving a stopgap spending bill instead, would lead to yet another shutdown. Congress and the White House will also likely need to negotiate another debt-ceiling increase early next year. Without agreement, the country would default for the first time in modern history, very likely plunging the economy into a tailspin. Not addressing the debt ceiling before the remainder of the $5 trillion in new borrowing authority approved by Republicans in last year’s “big, beautiful” law expires would limit the federal government to only spend what it brings in. That would lead to ramifications more significant than a government shutdown, including the possibility that Social Security checks would not go out on time and that medical providers wouldn’t be reimbursed for Medicare or Medicaid patients treatment.

articles.title: Advocacy group argues solar power can lighten costs for customers in Michigan with help of storage technology
articles.description: Tim Pawlenty from the Solar Energies Industry Association argues that Michigan's investment in solar battery storage makes the renewable energy source more reliable and appealing to consumers. The post Advocacy group argues solar power can lighten costs for customers in Michigan with help of storage technology appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: Tim Pawlenty from the Solar Energies Industry Association argues that Michigan’s investment in solar battery storage makes the renewable energy source more reliable and appealing to consumers. City schools, police stations, libraries and other municipal buildings get solar panels as part of DTE Energy’s MIGreenPower program. One advocacy group says Michigan has a solution to high energy costs: storing electricity in batteries powered by the sun. Former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty is the head of the non-profit Solar Energies Industry Association. He says Michigan is a leader in developing clean energy technology, though Pawlenty admits some residents have not quite seen the light yet. Tim Pawlenty: People have always wanted to know, “are you reliable?” In other words, when the sun isn’t shining, is there going to be energy for my house or for my business? These batteries answer that question. If you can have the storage through batteries be available when the sun isn’t shining to run your house or business, you’ve solved that reliability problem. The batteries used to be big and clunky and they didn’t have much storage in them. Now, they’ve gotten smaller; they’ve gotten more efficient in terms of technology and the price points have fallen. They can go from what used to be just a couple hours of storage all the way up to eight, 10 and soon to be probably 12 or 14 hours of storage…it’s started to change the whole entire concern about reliability of solar and storage in a very favorable way. Quinn Klinefelter: This is pretty new technology, then? TP: Well, batteries themselves (are) ancient technology, at least, ancient technology by today’s standards…the type of battery technology that’s evolving and coming onto the market, it’s just getting better and better. (It has a) longer and longer capacity for storage…the price points are dropping. I think the boom that you see in storage, helping to be led by Michigan, by the way, is not only going to continue, it’s going to accelerate. QK: Your group says that Michigan is one of the top states in the nation for using this type of battery storage. Do you get any sense as to why that would be? TP: Well, the top five for sure over the next few years is our projection…that’s really a leadership position…one of the reasons is you’ve got companies in Michigan that are investing and growing heavily. General Motors talked about their next generation vision talked about their next vision for batteries could be revolutionary in many respects. LG is building its second battery storage and manufacturing plant in Michigan…the list goes on. …I think because of the companies that already exist there, (in Michigan) their capabilities, their skill, their workforce…(Michigan) has really become a leader in battery storage technology and deployment of it. QK: If you’re trying to do this at scale, is increasing investment in this type of solar power particularly expensive? TP: Well, it is…there’s different buckets of solar and storage. Of course, there’s the residential, which we’re all familiar with. Panels on the house, battery in the garage. That’s number one. Number two is community solar which is sort of smaller project. Not on roofs but on the ground in communities for local use. That’s community solar. Three is commercial solar which is on top of Walmarts or large warehouse buildings on the roofs. More panels, bigger roofs. The last one is utility-scale solar, which is these large scale solar facilities that take up a lot of land but also produce an enormous amount of energy for the grid or for large industrial or commercial use…all of that together is the solar and storage industry. QK: Would homeowners need to have their own receptacle, their own battery? Or would it be something just kind of sent along the typical electric grid? TP: Well, you can have solar only on your house, but for people who can afford it or are interested in it, the battery in the garage can be a really good option because you can store the energy all day long using the panels. …at night, if you need it, you can use the battery you can use the battery and even charge up your car with it…and have those three things work together…In many cases, the batteries are getting so good that there’s extra energy in those batteries…people can get some financial benefit by selling it back to the grid. Now, that depends on local regulations and rules and laws and what the utilities allow and stuff like that…that home based ecosystem where you’re sort of your own supplier of your own energy is appealing to a lot of people. Putting a battery in there gives them that reliability factor as well. QK: With your past history as governor of Minnesota, you’re obviously very well versed in politics. President Trump has long criticized solar power, among many other clean energy initiatives. He’s pushed for fossil fuels and his administration has cut or scaled back clean energy credits. They withheld funding for some grants. They tried to block some solar competitions from coming from China. Even with a new congress controlled by Democrats coming in next year, do you foresee any of that opposition going away? TP: Well, I think the new congress is going to be more favorable to renewable energy, including solar and storage. Of course, President Trump is still there with the veto pen, but the fact remains: solar and storage are booming in the United States. I think that’s the market saying, not government necessarily saying, the market saying, “we want more of what you’ve got, because solar and storage is cost effective, quick to deploy…reliable with the batteries and storage and it’s also clean.” The market is saying that we want more of what you have to offer. That’s a powerful message. I think the president and congress hopefully will work together in a rational way. We’re not trying to say that solar and storage is the total answer. We’re for all of the above. We just think we can play an important role as one piece of the pie chart. QK: You’ve seen politics for a long time. Do you really think it’s possible for a divided government, whatever government can or can’t do for this, that they can work together in a “rational” way at this moment in time? TP: I think so for a few reasons. First of all, Iran can’t block the sun. When you’re worried about national security and global energy prices because it’s a global market, you know, having the ability to get something for free from the sun is such an appealing prospect. …Number two, the president and congress have to work together at some level. Neither wants to just sit there for two years and do nothing. There’s one opportunity right in front of us in this lame duck session. There’s a bipartisan permitting bill pending before congress right now that…could pass…and help speed up more projects, more things being built in America. We need that as a way to help create more supply to help hold down prices. TP: Lastly, in the context of some compromise, President Trump and this congress could find a way to mutually satisfy at least some of each others priorities and initiatives. President Trump, by the way, has endorsed that permitting bill I just mentioned. Even he, on a bipartisan basis, supports that. In Michigan, through LG, that battery plant I mentioned and GM of course, there’s a corning facility that makes component parts for the solar and storage industry…all of that adds up to this: solar and storage is an important part of the manufacturing renaissance in the United States. We want to bring more things related to the storage and solar supply chain back to America. We now supply hundreds of thousands of good paying jobs across this country. You are seeing investment in solar and storage facilities all across the country including in Michigan.

articles.title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
articles.description: CTIA said jamming test showed "interference... up to two and a half miles away."
articles.content: The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons. Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing: The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts. CTIA said the pilot test shows "that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications."Read full article Comments

articles.title: European troops from 11 countries hold a drill in Poland for a potential postwar Ukraine mission
articles.content: NOWA DEBA, Poland (AP) — Two suspected Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone entered Polish airspace Friday, near a military exercise involving thousands of European troops preparing for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine. Polish and other European officials viewed the incursion as a Kremlin warning against the drill. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said two of the objects were believed to be missiles and the third a jet-powered drone. They landed in southeastern Poland within tens of kilometers of Nowa Deba, the military training ground where the allied troops were drilling. “This was not an accidental event. It was closely coordinated with our show of force today,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said Friday at a news conference during the drills. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the airspace violation was likely an intentional provocation timed to coincide with the drill, an assessment that was echoed by the U.K. and French defense ministers attending the military exercises in Nowa Deba. On Thursday, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said he believed Russia was “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine. He and fellow U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff were in Berlin to reassure European leaders about U.S. President Donald Trump’s discussions on ending the nearly 5-year-old war at his historic trilateral talks Thursday with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. “The fundamental point that’s been proven overnight is that you have to judge Putin on what he does not on what he says,” U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told the AP in Nowa Deba. “This is a man who said he wouldn’t invade Ukraine only days before he invaded Ukraine.” Led by France and the United Kingdom, the multinational force is a non-NATO military initiative of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a wider political group of 37 nations supporting Ukraine. The two-week exercise, which began on Nov. 9, is for the first time checking this coalition’s ability to deploy in Ukraine once the war ends and help to stabilize the country and rebuild its military. It is aimed both at testing deployment plans and sending a message to Russia and the Trump administration that European countries are stepping up militarily. Around 2,800 personnel from Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and the U.K. are taking part in the exercise, with Poland providing the logistical backup. Turkey was participating remotely from Istanbul. French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that 1,100 troops from France were deployed, and that “we have terrestrial, air but also maritime operations, a dozen countries that are active in this coalition.” The exercise in Poland follows 12 months of planning by the Multinational Force-Ukraine, or MNF-U, said U.K. brigadier Campbell Close, who serves as deputy commander for operations of the French Army’s 1st division. That division is in charge of the land part of the “Koalicja” exercise in Poland. “This is a deployment exercise,” Close said on Monday in Nowa Deba. “We are a defensive force.” He praised Poland’s handling of the logistics of moving thousands of vehicles, people and their equipment for the drill. If deployed once a ceasefire is in place, the force would help regenerate Ukraine’s armed forces, provide the reassurance needed to open the country’s skies and help clear mines in the Black Sea, Lt. Gen. Tom Bateman, commander of MNF-U, has said. It would not have peacekeeping or peace-monitoring functions. Coalition troops arrived in Poland by sea, air and land, the Polish government said, before traveling by rail and road to the Nowa Deba training site. They rehearsed transporting personnel and equipment, as well as joint command-and-control exercises, and flew fighter jets and an aerial refueling tanker. They also operated surveillance drones, drilled responses to drone attacks and trained in trench warfare. The initial idea of the Coalition of the Willing was to provide Ukraine with security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5. In the absence of a NATO commitment to fulfill this function, France and the U.K. decided to go ahead with plans for a separate European proposal of countries willing to come to Ukraine’s aid if necessary. Last year, Putin said that any foreign troops inside Ukraine would be considered “legitimate targets.” The multinational troops may have a purely defensive function, but they would still need to be a “combat force for their own force protection,” said Ed Arnold, a senior associate fellow at the RUSI military think tank in London. Associated Press writers Jamey Keaten in Geneva and Stefanie Dazio and Geir Moulson in Berlin contributed to this report.

A Thanksgiving treat in the offing: Lower gas prices
articles.description: WASHINGTON — $3.62 a gallon. That’s the predicted national average price of regular gasoline on Thanksgiving Day, according to GasBuddy, which tracks prices at the pump. That would continue the steady glide path down that gasoline prices have followed for roughly the past month. Oversupply, worried consumers and seasonal driving trends have all contributed to the […]
articles.content: A gas pump in Indianapolis on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)WASHINGTON — $3.62 a gallon. That’s the predicted national average price of regular gasoline on Thanksgiving Day, according to GasBuddy, which tracks prices at the pump. That would continue the steady glide path down that gasoline prices have followed for roughly the past month. Oversupply, worried consumers and seasonal driving trends have all contributed to the drop. The price still would be high — in fact, a Thanksgiving record — by most standards. The highest Thanksgiving Day price average was reported in 2022, $3.56 a gallon. But by any measure, what’s happening now is good news for consumers. AAA reported Friday a gallon of regular gasoline cost an average $3.69, down 18 cents from a week ago and 58 cents from a month earlier. “For most holiday travelers, driving remains the cheapest and easiest way to get around” this Thanksgiving, said an AAA analysis. About 90% of travelers during the holiday are expected to drive. Anywhere they go, they should find prices lower than a few weeks ago. Prices tumbled in all 50 states over the past week. A dozen states’ averages fell more than 25 cents a gallon, according to GasBuddy. It found the biggest week-to-week drops in Montana, by 38.8 cents a gallon; Ohio, by 33.3 cents; Michigan, by 32.1 cents; Colorado, by 29.2 cents; and New Mexico, by 28.4 cents. The $4-a-gallon gasoline is also becoming less frequent. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, found 43 states’ prices for regular gasoline have fallen under that level. There are outliers, notably in states where the infrastructure makes it more difficult to get products. Hawaii had the highest gasoline prices Friday, at $5.60 a gallon for regular, followed by California at $5.50. The lowest price was in North Carolina at $3.03 per gallon The averages, though, don’t reflect highs and lows within states, which can vary. Why are prices down? Oil prices are down roughly $25 a barrel over the past month. Part of the explanation is hope that the U.S.-Iran war will soon end, or at least cool. “Markets bet on a de-escalation between the U.S. and Iran following the midterm elections,” said Grace Zwemmer, an economist at Oxford Economics. Each change of a dollar for a barrel of oil is estimated to mean about 2.5 cents per gallon at the retail level. Prior to the war, about 20% of the world’s oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway between Oman and Iran. Despite occasional skirmishes, that oil is mostly proceeding through the strait. The change in outlook is partly due to reduced demand and partly an expectation that the war’s impact will wane. “Expectations of a coming supply surplus outweighed fresh security incidents around the Strait of Hormuz,” De Haan said. The November report from the International Energy Agency saw the oil market engaged in “tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran.” The IEA predicted that the global oil market could return to a surplus in this quarter, “with a more substantial build in 2027.” The U.S. Energy Information Administration had similar forecasts. It predicted per-barrel oil prices averaging $84 next year, about the same as the current level, with retail gasoline prices averaging $3.56 a gallon. The prediction assumes that 2027 will proceed “as oil flows recover and inventories rebuild.” Goldman Sachs echoed that forecast, saying this week in an analysis that “oil is forecast to ease gradually in 2027 as suppliers in the Middle East adapt to disruption from the war in Iran.” Worried consumers Some causes of the price drop are seasonal. Americans tend to drive less in colder months, which means a drop in demand. And, said De Haan in an X post, “After Sept 15, stations can sell winter blend, which is cheaper to make. Summer gas has to meet tighter evaporation rules, and that costs refiners more.” At the same time, consumers have become more cautious about spending. The cost of living “continues to be at the forefront of consumers’ minds across the population,” said Joanne Hsu, director of the University of Michigan Survey of Consumers. The survey’s November report found that about 57% of consumers “spontaneously mentioned that their living standards have been eroded by high prices.” That’s the highest level since May, and higher than the 46% who felt that way in February before the war began. In the United States, the cooling demand is reflected in AAA’s projection that 72.9 million people are projected to drive somewhere during the holiday, down 200,000 from last year’s Thanksgiving season. An asterisk to all this cautious optimism: Oil prices are always hard to predict. A year ago no one saw the price spike that gripped the country this year. That’s why the international agency added this note in its analysis this month: “As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery.” And though the prices are down, they’re still historically high. “Americans aren’t letting the pump keep them from the table,” De Haan said, but “that doesn’t mean drivers aren’t feeling it.”

articles.title: 1% of particles in the air are plastic, U-M researchers say. Blame your tires
articles.description: The University of Michigan collected and analyzed air particles from school parking lots in southeast Michigan. Out of all the analyzed particles, 1% were made of plastic.
articles.content: The plastic problem is in the air. Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic that break down from larger pieces of plastic pollution, even things like microfibers from plastic-based clothing like polyester. Over a loud hum of several boxy grey instruments and a lurking fume hood glow, Abby Ayala and Kayleigh Reilly explained how to study invisible particles. Ayala is an atmospheric scientist and Reilly is an environmental chemist at the University of Michigan. “ Anything that’s in the atmosphere, we’re focusing on dry deposition. So the particles that are floating, land,” said Ayala. Great Lakes News Collaborative The Great Lakes region is blessed with an abundance of water. But water quality, affordability, and aging water infrastructure are vulnerabilities that have been ignored for far too long. In this series, members of the Great Lakes News Collaborative, Michigan Public, Bridge Michigan, Great Lakes Now, The Narwhal, and Circle of Blue, explore what it might take to preserve and protect this precious resource. This independent journalism is supported by the Charles Stewart Mott Foundation. She explained that they look at two kinds of particles, dust that lands on their samplers, and then an active sampler that can pull particles in for collection. The lab is filled floor to ceiling, every horizontal surface covered, every vertical surface with whiteboards and notes. It’s a vibrant postcard of active science. A new study from the University of Michigan, out last month, collected and analyzed air particles from school parking lots in southeast Michigan. Out of all the analyzed particles, 1% were made of plastic. Anne McNeil, an organic and polymer chemist at the University of Michigan and an author of the study, explained what that number can feel like. “I think people all react to this number differently if you tell them that 1% of all the particles in the air are plastic. For me, I’m like, ‘Oh, okay, that’s not that bad.’ Whereas other people are like, ‘Ah, I’m breathing in plastic.’”Donate Because 1% is a small percentage overall. But if it’s 1% of all of the air in the atmosphere? That can feel like a lot. Microplastics can get into the air from water and vice versa Microplastics are a pervasive pollutant in both the lakes and the oceans. The waterways and the atmosphere are connected. The best way to visualize this is to imagine a wave breaking on shore. The foam that forms is an active connection between water and air, and particles are being exchanged. Studies have found that the ocean can contribute a relatively small amount of plastic to the atmosphere, as well as receive microplastics from the air. University of Michigan researchers wanted to know if this process was also occurring in the Great Lakes. Related: Study: Washing machines send ‘toxic stew’ of microfibers into Great Lakes EPA move on microplastics, pharmaceuticals draws mixed response in Michigan Takeout trash is piling up at Michigan universities. There’s no easy fix Pure Michigan has a poop problem: Dangerous fecal levels befoul 3 of 4 rivers “ There was another polyethylene particle that’s like quite different. It’s got this, like, spherical morphology to it, so it’s more rounded. And when we look at the elemental mapping of that particle, we see calcium carbonate, which is a common salt that is in, like, the Great Lakes. And so, both the morphology being more like sphere-like and the salt, the presence of the salt from the lakes tells us that that particle likely also came from the lake when it was put into the air,” said McNeil. She said it was the first recorded evidence she knew of that the lakes were contributing to atmospheric microplastics. But the evidence was limited, and so the lakes are not currently considered a significant source of microplastics into the air. Tire particles are a much bigger contributor Tires, however, are a known major contributor of plastic particles in the air, and this study confirmed that. They found that tire particles contributed significantly more to the atmospheric plastic problem than other types of plastics. “You change the tires on your car because the tread wears down. Where do you think all that tread went, right? The friction of your heavy car moving across the concrete is wearing down those tires. And so all of those particles end up on the road and then the roadside. They get run over by other things, so they get smaller and smaller over time. And then, of course, the wind, and other modes of getting that into the air, can bring those tire particles up into the air,” said McNeil. A secondary, much smaller fraction of the particles found were from clothing fibers. “Where we are concerned is just the passive shedding of fibers off your clothes,” said Anna Schellin, an atmospheric chemist at the University of Michigan. “You ever pull out the lint trap and there’s a ton of lint on there? If you’re washing synthetic clothes, or drying synthetic clothes, rather, a lot of that is plastic material, but the lint trap is not capturing all of the lint that’s escaping the system,” said Schellin. Schellin was not part of the school parking lot study, but she is part of a collaborative team that is interested in understanding our atmosphere. She co-authored a paper last year that looked at major microplastic sources getting into the air in Michigan, using state-to-global level emissions data. The health impacts of a plastic polluted atmosphere are still being studied. Multiple studies have shown impacts to the lungs. And some of the particles found by McNeil and her colleagues were at the nano scale. Particles at that scale are small enough to be inhaled into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. This is still a very active area of research, with more studies in process to continue to examine how much plastic is getting into our air, where it is coming from, and, hopefully, how we can stop it.

articles.title: Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger
articles.description: Modeling predicts plume of neurotoxic lead could reach up to 100 miles away.
articles.content: In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week. The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week. "Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. "Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."Read full article Comments

Mayor Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
articles.content: Photo: Michael M. Santiago / Getty Images News / Getty Images New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Friday (November 20) that Rikers Island will close by the end of 2032 under his administration's plan to replace the jail complex with four borough-based facilities. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane,” Mamdani said in a statement. “This plan puts us on a path to deliver just that: closing Rikers, reducing pretrial detention, tackling the case delays that deprives people of their right to a speedy trial and investing $146 million in evidence-based supports that help break the cycles of incarceration.” In a video shared on social media Friday, Mamdani explained that the replacement jails would be closer to public transportation, making it easier for people in custody to reach family members, legal counsel and court proceedings. He also said the city would move people with serious mental health and medical needs from jails into hospitals for around-the-clock care. According to the Mayor's Office, the first replacement jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, followed by facilities in the Bronx and Queens in 2031 and Manhattan in 2032. The administration aims to reduce the city's jail population from approximately 6,600 people to no more than 4,100 by the end of 2032. The proposed timeline extends the city's existing legal deadline of August 31, 2027. The City Council must approve legislation to change that date. The administration's $146 million investment next fiscal year includes $50 million for programming inside jails, $76 million for community-based services and $16 million for crime victims and survivors, according to the Mayor's Office. The city also plans to add 236 therapeutic beds at hospitals in Brooklyn and the Bronx for people with serious mental health conditions and complex medical needs. Mamdani referenced Kalief Browder, whose death by suicide drew national attention to conditions at Rikers. Department of Correction Commissioner Stanley Richards, who also appeared in the video, reflected on the thousands of people who have been incarcerated there, including himself. Browder was 16 when he was arrested in 2010 and spent three years at Rikers awaiting trial, including nearly two years in solitary confinement. After prosecutors dropped the charges, he was released in 2013 and died by suicide two years later at age 22. The effort to close Rikers dates back to 2019, when the City Council passed legislation requiring the city to replace the complex with four smaller jails, The Guardian reported. The facility remains under federal court-ordered oversight amid longstanding concerns about violence, staffing shortages and dangerous conditions inside its facilities. “Our city is safest when our government refuses to accept failed approaches to public safety just because it's always been done this way,” Mamdani said. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President
articles.content: President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them. “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.” [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VD-KP5xTESY] Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.” Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative. Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks: > Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside. > We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind. > So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

articles.title: Ask ELi: An ELPS Teacher’s Husband Was Elected to the School Board. How Will Conflicts of Interest Be Handled?
articles.description: The board member will need to disclose the conflict and recuse himself from some votes.
articles.content: Earlier this week, Scott Farver was announced as the winner of the final open seat on the East Lansing Board of Education after running a successful write-in campaign. After Farver was elected, a reader wrote to East Lansing Info asking how the district and Farver can manage potential conflicts of interest, as he is married to an East Lansing Public Schools teacher. The reader cited relevant state law that requires disclosure and abstention if there is a conflict. The section of the state law cited by the reader states: “A member of the board of a school district … is presumed to have a conflict of interest if the member or his or her family member has a financial interest, or a competing financial interest, in the contract or other financial transaction or is an employee of the school district, intermediate school district, or public school academy.” With Farver’s wife, Erin, working as a fifth-grade teacher at Marble Elementary, ELi reached out to board member and attorney Chris Martin to ask if the law prevents Farver from serving. “It’s definitely a conflict,” Martin said in a phone interview. “[But] conflict does not prevent you from serving. You do have to be careful and I think disclosing and acknowledging the conflict is the first step, and then again, the second step would be remaining mindful of the conflict and, you know, recusing yourself or abstaining if there is a situation where where the conflict comes up in a discussion or a vote.” Martin said teacher contracts and discussions involving compensation are among the matters from which Farver will need to recuse himself. Farver responded promptly to a text message from ELi. “It’s not a secret that my wife is a teacher in the district,” he said. “I’ll be following all laws when it comes to these issues and abstain when necessary.” ELi also asked Farver about his responses to our questionnaire for school board candidates, in which he said he wants to ensure teachers are compensated for the “incredible work they do.” Farver said that while he cannot vote on compensation, he will continue to advocate for teachers. You don’t have to go back far to find a school board member who faced a similar conflict. Gary Holbrook, who was selected to fill a board vacancy in 2023, also has a wife who teaches in the district. Holbrook, who served on the board for about 16 months, told ELi in a text message that he had to recuse himself only once or twice when the board considered teacher compensation. “There’s another side to that coin though,” he added. “It’s important for board members to have access to feedback across the stakeholder spectrum. Because I would occasionally meet with my wife’s colleagues for her work events, they had an opportunity to ask questions about how the board works and provide feedback in a low-stakes environment. There are some things the board does for reasons that aren’t immediately clear. They might be mandated activities or the topic might have a longer history than casual observers realize. On balance, having a board member with one foot in the school community is much more beneficial than detrimental.” Subscribing to an RSS feed requires an RSS browser plugin or the use of a news aggregator app or website.

articles.title: Expect University of Michigan's next athletic director to clean house, John U. Bacon says
articles.description: Aidan Hutchinson is out. How will the Detroit Lions' defense respond? Also, is change coming to the Michigan football program? Michigan Public's John U. Bacon weighs in.
articles.content: Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham glances at the scoreboard against Michigan State in the fourth quarter of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, in Ann Arbor, Mich. (AP Photo/Lon Horwedel)(Lon Horwedel/AP Photo/Lon Horwedel / FR170538 AP)The Detroit Lions lost their best defensive player last weekend.And the University of Michigan appears to be set to add a new athletic director.Meanwhile, Detroit Red Wings center Dylan Larkin is losing a lot of money every day. For more on that, Michigan Public sports commentator John U. Bacon joined Morning Edition host Doug Tribou.Doug Tribou: Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson is done for the season. During the Lions’ game in Germany against the New England Patriots, Hutchinson sacked Patriots quarterback Drake Maye. To celebrate, he leaped in the air and landed with both feet on the ground, but only one of his ACL’s intact. That knee injury will require surgery. Could you give us some perspective on how much Hutchinson means to the Lions defense?John U. Bacon: Almost everything. He's the captain of the team. He is their best defender by far. Two time All-Pro. But it must be said, after his gruesome leg injury two years ago, the Lions did go 15-2. They just didn't have enough to win a playoff game. So I could be wrong. And Doug, everybody loves it when I am wrong — including me, it should be noted. But I do not see this — anymore — as a Super Bowl-winning team without Hutchinson.DT: The Lions are one of three NFC North teams with a 7-2 record, along with the (Minnesota) Vikings and (Chicago) Bears. And things are about to get very busy for Detroit. Just back from Germany, the Lions will host Tampa Bay on Sunday afternoon. Then they’ll play their annual Thanksgiving Day game on Thursday when the Bears come to town. What will you be watching for in this critical stretch?JUB: Well, they should beat a weak Tampa Bay team pretty handily, but Chicago will be a real test for Detroit's defense. If they can handle the Bears without Hutchinson, they might have a chance.DT: In college football, Oregon beat up on Michigan last weekend in Oregon. Now the Ducks are coming to East Lansing to face the Spartans on Friday night. The Spartans are coming off a loss to Washington and are just 3-7 this year. Oregon is ranked 13th in the nation. What do you think MSU head coach Pat Fitzgerald can hope to achieve in their last two games?JUB: They already know they cannot make a bowl game, so they're playing for pride now. And for the players on this year's team, probably a spot on next year's team. These days, with automatic transfers, even the players can't take anything for granted. But from what I've seen so far, Fitz's team will play hard.DT: Meanwhile, Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham’s schedule isn’t getting any easier. After facing Oregon last week, now undefeated UCLA, No. 4 in the nation, is coming to the Big House Saturday afternoon. The Wolverines are 5-5 and have looked lost on offense even after the firing of offensive coordinator Jason Beck. Do you see any path to a late-season bright spot here, John?JUB: I think we're down to Jim Carrey in Dumb and Dumber: "So you're saying there's a chance?" That's about the chance you have here. The only thing that keeps me from saying this season is entirely over is two years ago, at 5-5, like they are now, Michigan somehow upset Northwestern and then somehow beat a far superior Ohio State team. That morning, I tweeted that Michigan had a 2% chance. So in the interest of inflation, I'll give Michigan a 3% chance this year. How's that?DT: [Laughs] The University of Michigan hasn’t made it official, but according to many media reports, U-M will soon have a new athletic director. Trev Alberts, who is currently the A.D. at Texas A&M, has reportedly accepted the job. Current AD Warde Manuel is on his way out at the end of the calendar year. What do you think Alberts will do?JUB: Well, he's earned a reputation as a chainsaw athletic director at Nebraska and at Texas A&M, firing both football head coaches despite massive buyouts. So, Doug, if I'm coach Kyle Whittingham, I don't think I'm buying a house this week. So expect Alberts to clean house. And probably beyond football, too.DT: Red Wings center Dylan Larkin is still not playing and still has not been traded, as he would like. He left the team in late October. The Wings suspended his pay. A website tracking his salary says he’s losing $41,000 a day and is approaching a million in lost wages so far. I guess that's good work if you can get… or not get it… or something like that. I'm not sure what the phrase is here. [Laughs]JUB: [Laughs] It's something like that. Yes, Doug, our analysis is spot on, as usual. Look, I'm not his agent, but that might not be a great business model, what he's pursuing currently. Unless, of course, what? He's going to get him on volume. I'm not clear.Editor's note: Some quotes in this article have been lightly edited for length and clarity. You can play the full audio of the interview near the top of this page.The University of Michigan holds Michigan Public's broadcast license.

articles.title: Straight-ticket voting surges in Michigan, testing party strategies
articles.description: Michigan has been a state of split-ticket voters. That seems to be changing. Here's why.
articles.content: (Kalloli Bhatt)Michigan has had a longstanding history of split-ticket voters.In 2002, voters elected Democrat Jennifer Granholm as governor and Republican Mike Cox as attorney general. In 2014, Michiganders elected Republican Rick Snyder as governor and Democrat Gary Peters to the U.S. Senate.But this year was a little different. In the 2026 midterm election, more Michiganders voted straight ticket than in the past 80 years.That’s according to Craig Mauger, state politics reporter for The Detroit News. He broke down how he figured out the trend and what it means for the state in a recent interview with Stateside.He said in the past, you would hear voters say “Hey, I’m going to look at this governor’s race and here’s why I like this candidate. Here’s why I like this candidate for attorney general.”How do we know Michiganders voted straight-ticket?Mauger examined two indicators: the number of straight-ticket ballots cast and how similarly Democratic candidates performed across statewide races.The first showed an increase in voters selecting a single party on their ballots.“We saw that the number of straight ticket ballots had gone up way above the increased voter turnout from 2022 to 2026,” Mauger said.He found, in the 69 counties he could get data for, straight-ticket voting went up 18% overall. Democratic straight-ticket voting rose by 20% and Republican straight-ticket voting increased by 15%.So, while Democrats saw substantial gains in the 2026 election, the increase in straight-ticket voting wasn’t exclusive to them, meaning it wasn’t just a wave of blue voters casting one-party ballots.Look to the spreadThe second indicator looked at the difference in support between Michigan’s best-performing and worst-performing Democratic candidates in statewide races.Mauger found that the spread between the two (Governor-Elect Jocelyn Benson and Attorney General-Elect Eli Savit) was just 2.04%.“That is the smallest spread that we were able to find since Michigan approved its current constitution in 1963,” he said. “So, that's where you're getting that 80-year period.”Essentially, Democratic candidates at the top of the ticket received remarkably similar levels of support, regardless of which office they were running for.That’s in comparison to past elections, when candidates from the same party could perform significantly differently from one another.“You would see spreads in elections that were like 20 point differences,” Mauger said. “One Democrat candidate would get 20 points more than the other. You're not seeing that in the last two elections.”Why are Michiganders sticking with one party?Well, there isn’t necessarily one explanation.Mauger said as voter turnout increases, so do the odds of people casting straight-ticket ballots. He also said a change in news-consumption culture might have played a role.“It used to be people would go home and watch the nightly news and they'd get kind of an objective recap,” he said. “They'd get their newspaper and get this objective analysis of what's happening. Now, a lot of times people go home and watch cable news and it's different.”The shift may also reflect how national politics increasingly shapes voters’ decisions in state and local races.Rather than evaluating candidates solely on their individual platforms or records, voters may be using their feelings about national political figures, like President Trump, to guide their decisions further down the ballot. And that could have significant implications for both political parties in Michigan.Future thinkingRegardless of what’s motivating the trend, Mauger said Republicans have some thinking to do.“They have to sit there and realize that they have not had a statewide candidate in Michigan,” he said. “At the top of the ticket, a partisan candidate for the Republicans has not gotten over 50% of the vote since 2014.”That doesn’t mean this trend is necessarily good news for Democrats, either. An electorate that votes more consistently along party lines could benefit either party, depending on the political environment and which voters turn out.It also raises a larger question about Michigan’s political identity.Michigan is still a swing state, with competitive elections and voters from both major parties. But being a swing state doesn’t necessarily mean voters are willing to cross party lines.And if Michiganders are increasingly voting for parties rather than individual candidates, future elections may depend less on persuading voters to split their tickets and more on which party can get its supporters to the polls.Until next time,Kalloli Bhatt, Digital Content Producer_______________________Have questions about Michigan politics? Or, just want to let us know what you want more of (less of?) in the newsletter? We always want to hear from you! Shoot us an email at politics@michiganpublic.org!__________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________Today’s newsletter was written by Kalloli Bhatt, and produced and edited by Michelle Keller.

articles.description: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Thursday passed a major bipartisan bill to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects. The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities. The […]
articles.content: Power lines at the Algodones Electric Generating Station between Rio Rancho and Santa Fe, New Mexico. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Thursday passed a major bipartisan bill to overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects. The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities. The bill would shorten environmental review times and narrow the criteria for triggering the comprehensive reviews required under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA. The measure gained approval of most Senate Republicans, who generally support streamlining environmental reviews, and several Democrats who want to see shorter review times for renewable-energy projects. Opponents voiced concern that NEPA, a bedrock federal statute for environmental protection, would be too severely weakened and that tribes would lose power over the consultation process. Just two Republicans — Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley and South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds — voted against the bill. On the flip side, only 15 members of the Democratic caucus voted in favor. The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee’s leaders — GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island — along with the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chair, GOP Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and ranking Democrat, Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, negotiated the measure. In a statement celebrating the bill’s passage, Capito said the upper chamber “took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people.” Capito said she has “spent years trying to achieve bipartisan compromise on legislation that gets our nation back to building,” adding that the bill “is the culmination of those efforts.” In his own statement, Heinrich said the measure would bring down electricity costs while preserving environmental standards. The bill “will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation,” the New Mexico Democrat said. President Donald Trump has backed the measure, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. In a statement of administration policy this month, the administration said the bill would “deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and economic growth across the United States.” ‘Deeply disappointing’ But the bill has drawn sharp criticism from many environmental organizations, including the Center for Western Priorities, a public lands group. The Center’s executive director, Aaron Weiss, described the vote as “deeply disappointing,” adding that senators “who promised Westerners they would stand up for our public lands just voted for a bill that sells them out to Big Oil and Big Tech.” Weiss urged the House to reject the bill and allow the next Congress beginning in early January to craft “a permitting bill that builds clean energy without sacrificing America’s public lands.” In the lower chamber, House Natural Resources Committee Chair Bruce Westerman said the Senate vote marked “a strong step forward in fixing our nation’s permitting challenges,” in a statement Friday. The Arkansas Republican said he looks forward “to working with my colleagues in the House to swiftly pass this bipartisan bill that will unleash the full force of American innovation.”

Inside Michigan whitefish rescue: late nights, high hopes and extracted sperm
articles.description: State scientists are mounting a last-ditch effort to prevent the iconic fish from extinction in Lake Michigan. The genetic rescue hopes to preserve future generations. It begins with a shock during spawning season.
articles.content: With Lake Michigan whitefish on the brink of collapse, state scientists executed a last-ditch rescue mission Working from a pier in Muskegon, they netted wild whitefish in hopes of raising their fertilized eggs in captivity for the foreseeable future Invasive mussels have the fish struggling for survival in the lower Great Lakes MUSKEGON — Anticipation is high for Michigan’s moonshot effort to save whitefish from the lower Great Lakes before they’re gone for good. But plans are coming together so hastily, Matt Hughes needed to call a supplier for a rush order on special chemicals so the fish that fed generations can survive in his hatchery. “I need you to overnight this to me,” the Michigan Department of Natural Resources hatchery biologist told his supplier Wednesday morning. Hours later, Hughes sped to a pier in Muskegon to collect eggs that would be housed in the Wolf Lake Fish Hatchery that very same night. Such is life lately for tribal, state and federal officials mounting a frantic effort to preserve Lake Michigan’s struggling whitefish stocks by raising their offspring in captivity Related: With no time to spare, Michigan hatches a Great Lakes whitefish rescue plan Michigan lawmakers may fund last-ditch effort to save whitefish Research starved of funds as whitefish vanish With whitefish disappearing, time for a Noah’s Ark strategy? With little time to spare, they’ve spent recent weeks scouting for available hatchery space, retrofitting equipment, securing funding and readying boats and supplies. It’s hectic, sure, but also “awesome,” Hughes told Bridge Michigan. “I’ve never gotten to raise whitefish. So it’s a new challenge, for a good cause that I’m excited about.” The hope is that captive-raised fish could eventually repopulate the lakes once humans find a way to quell the quagga mussels that now blanket the bottom of every Great Lake except Superior. The mussels hog the lakes’ nutrients, plunging commercial harvests of whitefish from 6.9 million pounds in 2009 to less than 2 million today.Donate With baby whitefish dying of starvation soon after hatching, scientists believe most of the whitefish left in the lower lakes will soon die of old age. Efforts to intervene were limited until this summer, when following extensive reporting by Bridge Michigan, state lawmakers allocated $350,000 and the Great Lakes Fishery Trust chipped in nearly $900,000 more. That triggered a race to prepare for a “genetic rescue” mission during the November spawning season. In addition to the state DNR work in Muskegon, officials with the Little Traverse Bay Bands Of Odawa Indians will rescue fish from northern Lake Michigan. Bridge Michigan observed the operation on an unseasonably warm November night. The effort began at a moment’s notice, after DNR officials heard reports that anglers were catching ripe whitefish off the breakwall where Muskegon Lake meets Lake Michigan. That signaled that the fish, which normally stay in deep waters, have gone near shore to spawn. A crew of more than a dozen people rushed to the scene. “It’s all hands-on-deck right now,” said Patrick Hanchin, who manages the state’s Charlevoix Fisheries Research Station. “Everybody who can help is here.” Working out of a small boat in the Muskegon Channel, crews placed gillnets in the water for short increments, careful to retrieve the fish before they endured too much stress. The fish were transferred into holding pens in the channel, before crews moved the fertile ones into large plastic tubs, keeping males and females separate. State workers worked late in the night and into the following day, netting 40 fertile males and females to be spawned pair-by-pair and transferred to Wolf Lake. It could be a tough effort. The whitefish are believed to be about 20, making them elderly and lowering odds of reproducing. So crews tried not to stress out the fish. In some cases, they used “electrofishing,” shocking them briefly to render them unconscious, rather than snagging them in nets and making them struggle. Along with fish, the nets hauled invasive mussels out of the water. Voracious filter-feeders, the mussels have stripped the lower Great Lakes of plankton that are a key food source for baby whitefish and a host of other species. The lakes’ magnificent clarity is a sign of an ecosystem largely devoid of life. As the rescue unfolded nearby, Dennis LeMaire jigged for whitefish off the pier. Back when whitefish were abundant, the docks would be packed nearly shoulder-to-shoulder with anglers during the fall spawning season, LeMaire said. Now, it’s much lonelier. Once the fish were netted, Hughes — who hours earlier was working the phones for supplies — sprung into action to extract their eggs and sperm. Water triggers fertilization, a process crews didn’t want to start prematurely. So the female fish were dried with a towel before Hughes pressed on their bellies to release thousands of eggs into a metal bowl. Next, a few drops of sperm were squeezed from a male fish, before Hughes used a feather to gently mix the gametes. Water from the hatchery was then added to trigger fertilization. The fertilized eggs were transferred to a plastic container dosed with an iodine-based disinfectant, where they soaked for 30 minutes before being moved to a new container. “That’s going to kill anything on the outside or inside of the egg that we don’t want in a hatchery,” Hughes said. This process was repeated 40 times, with each set of eggs kept separate to avoid cross-contamination. The parents die in the process. Their carcasses will be shipped to Michigan State University for a health analysis. Among other things, scientists will check for disease, alerting the state to any infected fish so their eggs can be discarded to keep the hatchery disease-free. After fertilization, the crew had 24 hours until the developing eggs would become too delicate to be handled. So late at night, Hughes and colleagues drove to Wolf Lake hatchery to place them in cold water incubators where they’ll remain for the next several weeks. “We just hope they do well in the hatchery,” Hanchin said. One challenge: The state has little experience raising whitefish. Michigan devotes little taxpayer money to fish and wildlife management efforts, instead funding it primarily with recreational hunting and fishing license dollars. In turn, the DNR has mostly devoted its hatcheries to game fish like salmon and walleye. While recreational anglers target whitefish during the fall spawning run, the species is primarily considered a commercial catch. So state officials looked to Michigan’s tribes for advice about the genetic rescue. Several, including the Little Traverse Bands of Odawa Indians and Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, have run experimental hatchery programs for years and have long advocated for the state and federal governments to devote more resources to whitefish recovery. If and when the fish develop to the point that their eyes are visible through their egg shells, they’ll be moved to the Jordan River National Fish Hatchery in Elmira to continue growing. For now, it’s not clear what will happen from there. Ideally, officials say, at least some of them would remain in human care for years or even decades until the mussel invasion subsides, serving as a broodstock for future reintroduction efforts. But current funding will cover only a couple of years of hatchery space, fish food and other expenses. And efforts to quell the Great Lakes mussel invasion – a necessary prerequisite to restoring wild whitefish stocks – are similarly short on funds. Leaders of the rescue effort hope to recruit deeper-pocketed partners, such as neighboring states and the US and Canadian governments, to continue and expand the program. “Fingers crossed,” Hanchin said.
