Running for US Senate leader, Van Hollen backs ending filibuster but wouldn’t force it
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Maryland Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is seeking the role of majority leader, clarified Thursday that while he would personally like to get rid of the rule that requires at least 60 lawmakers vote to move forward on a bill, he believes the final call isn’t up to him. “I said […]
articles.content: U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat, spoke to then-state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, who at the Polk County Democrats Steak Fry in Des Moines, Iowa, on Sep. 13, 2025. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)WASHINGTON — Maryland Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is seeking the role of majority leader, clarified Thursday that while he would personally like to get rid of the rule that requires at least 60 lawmakers vote to move forward on a bill, he believes the final call isn’t up to him. “I said my personal view has been that the filibuster is anti-democratic because you can only end a filibuster — currently, you need 60 votes,” he said. “So that allows, you know, 41 senators to block the will of the majority. So, yes, I’m in favor of filibuster reform. How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.” Van Hollen announced earlier this month that he will challenge New York Sen. Chuck Schumer, who has led Democrats in that chamber for nearly a decade, for the role of majority leader in the next Congress. Schumer has said repeatedly since then that he is “confident” he has the votes to remain the top Senate Democrat for the next two years. Van Hollen’s comments about the filibuster came during an afternoon press conference where he, Oregon Sen. Jeff Merkley and Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine discussed how to restructure rules to move bills through that chamber faster. Merkley and retiring Republican Sen. Steve Daines released a detailed list of proposed changes to Senate rules in October that they believe will help the chamber function better. Talking filibuster Those suggestions would not eliminate the 60-vote legislative filibuster but were designed to “increase the Senate’s capacity to process legislation, increase amendments considered on the floor, and strengthen the power of the committees, all while upholding the constitutional design and distinctive characteristics of the Senate.” Merkley said during the press conference he would like to see the legislative filibuster change so that if a lawmaker “says they want more debate, they actually have to debate.” “That debate has to be sustained day and night, through the weekend, through the recess,” he said. “On simple bills, that vision would result in the filibuster ending because when there’s a break in debate, it ends.” The Senate does allow for talking filibusters, like the one New Jersey Democratic Sen. Cory Booker undertook in April 2025, but those are not used nearly as often as the 60-vote legislative filibuster that Merkley and Van Hollen said they’d like to overhaul. In addition to debating what to do with procedural votes, Van Hollen said he supports the Daines-Merkley rule changes because it would help the Senate to function better, especially as it welcomes a new group of freshman senators. “One of the things we’ve seen over the years, many years, is a concentration of power in just one person in the Senate, the leader. Both the Republican leader or the Democratic leader, which of course disempowers the committees,” Van Hollen said. “And if we really want senators to be able to have meaningful input, we need to make sure that the product of their work is actually considered and given a vote in the United States Senate.” Van Hollen declined to say how many votes he has secured for his majority leader bid, which Senate Democrats will decide in a closed-door vote on Dec. 1. “I’m in this to win it, and so that is my goal,” he said. “Because I think if we want to move forward on an ambitious agenda like this, we do need new leadership. We need to change the culture of the Democratic Caucus. People need to have more meaningful input. Our new members need to be at the table.”

articles.title: US Senate GOP tanks new resolution blocking Trump’s war in Iran
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Nearly all U.S. Senate Republicans on Thursday again blocked a House-passed War Powers Resolution to stop President Donald Trump’s war with Iran unless expressly authorized by Congress, sending mixed messages on the unpopular conflict after both GOP-led chambers passed a similar measure earlier this year. The vote marked the first chance for lawmakers […]
articles.content: Sen. Adam Schiff of California, left, and Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, both Democrats, talk to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 6, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Nearly all U.S. Senate Republicans on Thursday again blocked a House-passed War Powers Resolution to stop President Donald Trump’s war with Iran unless expressly authorized by Congress, sending mixed messages on the unpopular conflict after both GOP-led chambers passed a similar measure earlier this year. The vote marked the first chance for lawmakers to take a stand on the record regarding the Iran war since voters delivered abysmal losses for Republicans in the midterms. Americans, who have watched gas and diesel prices skyrocket since the conflict began, repeatedly expressed disapproval for the Iran war in public polls before and after the November election. The largely symbolic measure on the Senate floor Thursday, called a concurrent resolution, does not require the president’s signature or carry the force of law behind it. Trump ignored a similar War Powers Resolution cleared by Congress June 23. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., one of the most vocal proponents of the Iran War Powers Resolutions, said Trump has an obligation to listen to lawmakers and voters. “Who has the power to declare war? Only one branch, Article One. When both houses have said this war is illegal: Stop it, or get an authorization. The president can’t veto the Constitution,” Kaine said Thursday outside the Senate chamber. “The American people have spoken even more loudly about why this is such a bad idea,” he added. The measure, H.Con.Res. 93, sponsored in the House by Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., failed the Senate by a vote of 48-51. Origins of resolutions Congress created the measure during the Vietnam War era to rein in President Richard Nixon’s military campaign in Southeast Asia that resulted in tens of thousands of American service member deaths, and Vietnamese civilian deaths in estimates from hundreds of thousands to millions. The handful of Republican senators who voted in favor of Thursday’s Iran War Powers Resolution included Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Susan Collins of Maine, who recently lost her bid for reelection. The trio have consistently voted in favor of directing Trump to stop his Middle East military campaign. Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman voted no, continuing his streak of opposing an Iran War Powers Resolution more than a dozen times. Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut was absent, as he is recovering from a stroke. Cassidy and Tillis When the House-passed measure squeaked by in the Senate in June, Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy joined Collins, Murkowski and Paul in supporting the symbolic resolution. At that time Cassidy was just over a month out from losing the Republican primary in Louisiana after Trump endorsed one of his opponents. The Louisiana Republican voted against the War Powers Resolution Thursday. Similarly, in September, Cassidy opposed a House-passed Iran War Powers Resolution that failed on the Senate floor in a 49-50 vote. During that Sept. 24 vote, Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who is retiring, joined Collins, Murkowski and Paul in supporting the measure. Tillis cast a “no” vote Thursday. Tillis announced his retirement last year after Trump publicly threatened to primary him when the North Carolina senator voted against the president’s “one big beautiful” tax and spending cuts package. Tillis’ and Cassidy’s offices did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Pulling war funding? Kaine said Democrats, who assume the majority in the Senate in January, are looking for a different path to stop the Iran war. “We can’t make a president follow the law if he’s going to violate the law. So when we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we’re actually contemplating things in connection with the (continuing resolution funding) discussion,” Kaine said. Lawmakers have until Dec. 11 to approve a stopgap funding bill to keep the government functioning. Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., the chamber’s highest ranking Democratic appropriator, said on the Senate floor Thursday that a Democratic Congress “means Donald Trump is absolutely not getting his one-and-a-half trillion-dollar war budget, or the nearly $70 million he wants to bankroll the Iran war.” “There is no way on God’s green earth that I’m going to let Republicans jam through a funding bill that blows war spending through the roof,” she said.

articles.content: Owosso residents held a vigil on Nov. 19, 2026, honoring two homeless people and a dog found dead in a tent. (Photo Erick Diaz Veliz/Michigan Advance)Tyler Beebe enjoyed taking walks around the homeless encampment in Owosso, located between South Cedar and Cass avenues, recalled 45-year-old Reanna Denter. “Are you looking for treasures? Because there are treasures everywhere,” she remembers him always saying before inviting her to go for a walk. Denter is one of about 10 people living in the encampment where Tyler Beebe, Amy Hicks and her dog, Luna, were found dead in their tents on Nov. 16. On Thursday afternoon, dozens gathered a short distance from the encampment for a candlelight vigil honoring Beebe, Hicks and Luna. The vigil brought together residents, volunteers, religious leaders and people who have experienced homelessness. Beyond remembering those who died, participants called attention to the difficulties of finding permanent housing, accessing mental health services and other social services, and surviving outdoors during Michigan’s cold months. “There is no progress,” Nicole Bryant, 26, said. “Cities are trying to evict people who are homeless from their encampments. Lansing’s the same way. People just got removed from their campsite out there. They’re basically putting a band-aid over a bullet hole. Some of these people just got kicked out of their house, or their house burned down, or something that they can’t even prevent.” “There’s a lot of hate on the homeless out here, a lot, and it’s not their fault for being homeless,” she finished. (Photo Erick Diaz Veliz/Michigan Advance) Bryant, a friend of Beebe, who recently experienced homelessness herself, described the daily challenges of living without a permanent place to stay, including finding food, accessing showers, obtaining clean clothes, and securing a safe place to sleep. She also pointed to long waiting periods for housing assistance, estimating it could take about a year to access that support. Bryant said Beebe had been trying to find housing but struggled to access available assistance. The circumstances surrounding the deaths remain under investigation. Police said they found a heating source, including an unventilated propane tank, inside the tent. In a statement shared with media outlets, City Manager Nathan Henne said the city is part of the Owosso Emergency Warming Center, participates in its organizational meetings and commits resources if necessary. “The warming center’s most common challenge is a lack of volunteers to staff the nightly shifts,” he says. “Owosso officers routinely encourage people living outdoors to seek help from local resources, including the warming center, Homeless Angels and Jennifer’s Place. However, each provider has its own admission rules and resource limits that are difficult for some to abide by.” And for people currently living in encampments, the need for assistance is immediate. Patty Bixby, a community volunteer with approximately 10 years of experience supporting people in need, said more resources and volunteers are necessary to address the situation. “The needs are monetary funds and volunteering,” Bixby said. “It really takes a village to be able to help all these people. This is just one encampment. There are several in this community, and the city isn’t doing enough.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE As winter approaches, the vigil served both as a memorial and a call for action. Deanna Aldrich, 62, a community member who organized the vigil, said she wanted to bring residents together after learning about the deaths and recognizing the need for a broader community response to this issue. “Homeless people need to have some programs in place,” Aldrich highlighted. “People say, ‘Okay, here’s where you can go get food,’ but we need some programs to help them. Maybe they don’t know how to read or write. Maybe they don’t know how to fill out an application. Maybe they don’t have a phone. Maybe they don’t have a physical address that they can use to get a job. Maybe they have a felony charge, and nobody’s going to hire them.” “I just want people to be aware,” she added. “It’s going to start getting colder, and they’re working diligently to open the shelter and the churches overnight. But we need people. We need people to supervise that and to be willing to spend some time.”

‘I agree with the president’: incoming senator Abdul El-Sayed seeks to help Trump end military aid to Israel
articles.content: Michigan senator-elect also secured a meeting with JD Vance, who called him a ‘terrible evil’ in lead-up to election The incoming US senator Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said that he and Donald Trump were in agreement about ending foreign military aid to Israel – and he hopes to find more common ground with the US president when he takes office. “I agree with the president – I can’t believe I’m saying that – that we need to end foreign military aid that is unconditional to Israel, as well as Egypt and Saudi Arabia and Pakistan,” the senator-elect said. In a surprise election day announcement, Trump told Fox News that the US would end military aid to Israel at the end of this year under an agreement reached with that country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “I think we need to be applying very basic international law to what Israel is and has been doing,” El-Sayed added. “We should not continue to be running cover for them at the UN, at the ICC, at the ICJ.” He said he wanted to see Congress change its posture on the US’s relationship with Israel, starting by making sure the Democratic caucus is no longer funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby that spent heavily against El-Sayed in his election. The comments come after El-Sayed said he has secured a meeting with JD Vance. The senator would not share the agenda of the meeting, but confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff reached out to him after his election victory. El-Sayed has goaded the Trump administration into working with him. In recent days, he created a shiny gold “TrumpCare” card and said that Trump can call Medicare for All “TrumpCare” if it will help expand healthcare to more Americans. Vance regularly attacked El-Sayed on the campaign trail, calling the incoming senator a “terrible evil” and “corrupted”. After El-Sayed won his race, he called Vance “habibi”, a term of endearment in Arabic, and joked about how the vice-president will have to preside over his swearing-in ceremony in January. During an interview earlier this week on Fox, Vance said that if El-Sayed wants to work with the Trump administration “to make people’s lives better”, then he would find “very much a willing partner”. El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim US senator in January, overcame tens of millions of dollars spent against him, first in a closely watched primary and then a swing-state general election. He has three immediate goals once he’s sworn in, he told the Guardian: stopping the “nuclear bomb” of Medicaid cuts, ending the war in Iran and addressing the “stupid approach” to tariffs. He also plans to propose Medicare for All legislation, get to work on voting rights legislation after the US supreme court gutted the Voting Rights Act, advance the Pro Act to expand union rights and overturn Citizens United, the supreme court decision that unleashed unfettered outside spending on campaigns. El-Sayed is supporting the Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen’s bid for the Senate leadership role. El-Sayed said Van Hollen, an advocate for Palestinian rights, would be an “amazing leader, and he’s a departure from a lot of the instincts of the past”. Van Hollen was an early supporter of El-Sayed in his primary election against the US representative Haley Stevens and campaigned for El-Sayed. As part of his campaign promise to change the Washington establishment, El-Sayed said he would not be moving his family to the US capital, and would be spending a lot of time back in Michigan doing town halls and talking to voters. El-Sayed has two young daughters. He’s one of a large group of incoming senators and representatives who skewed younger this cycle and also have young children. The “somewhat erratic” schedule of the job makes it harder on people with kids, he said, so making the US Capitol building a “free and open place” for children would help. The Capitol should help “good senators and congresspeople also be good parents”, he said. “I think one of the challenges with service is that we forget that every public servant is a private servant too, and that’s to their families, in particular to their children,” El-Sayed said. “And those two things shouldn’t be mutually exclusive.” Throughout his campaign, El-Sayed faced Islamophobic rhetoric, including from Trump and Republican officials. Though his campaign wasn’t about defending himself, Michiganders rejected those attacks when they voted him in, and that was important, he said. “There are a lot of kids who are watching,” he said. “And when the president of the United States is attacking somebody for their name or how they pray, it’s important that the people of the state of Michigan stood up and said, ‘No, this is not how we want to be.’ And I think they sent a message that was loud and clear, and I’m really grateful for that.”

Combatting adversarial distillation
articles.description: OpenAI’s layered approach to adversarial distillation combines model training, safeguards, detection, and enforcement to protect against capability extraction.
articles.content: How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry. As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked. We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry. Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity. We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. We’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards. Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them. The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked. Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities. In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to users—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces. We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments. After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.1 Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes. We defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards. Our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards. Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners. We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses. Tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller. API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning. With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning. When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services. This work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments. Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models. To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss. We also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well. GPT‑6 Astra defender with original safeguards GPT‑6.2 Astra defender with updated safeguards Extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request Extracting protected reasoning from the current request Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better. We have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer. In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to new attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations. Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place.
